Preface 0.1 Who this book is for I wrote this book for students in epidemiology or population health sciences working toward a PhD who want to move from associational thinking to causal thinking. I assume you have had an introductory course in epidemiology and one in biostatistics — you should be comfortable with concepts like confounding, odds ratios, and hazard ratios, and with fitting a regression model. I do not assume any prior exposure to causal inference as a formal framework, and I do not assume any prior experience with R. We will develop both over the course of the book. 0.2 How the book works The ideas in this book are easier to learn when they are attached to a real analysis, so we will return throughout to two running examples drawn from the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NAMCS). The first asks whether treatment with a selective Cox-2 inhibitor, compared with a nonselective NSAID, changes the risk of peptic ulcer disease. The second asks whether initiating a statin changes the risk of a cardiovascular event, and brings in follow-up time, censoring, and survival outcomes. As we work through these examples, we will also build a small toolkit of R functions for estimating causal effects, including standardization, propensity score weighting, and censoring weights, which you will write once and then reuse and extend in later chapters. 0.3 Software Appendix A walks through installing R, RStudio, and the packages this book relies on, including a companion package that provides the NAMCS example datasets in a de-identified, teaching-ready form. You can install that package directly from GitHub: remotes::install_github("alanbrookhart/NAMCS") If you run into trouble at any point, Appendix A is the place to look first.

Chapter 1 Why causal inference? 1.1 Questions epidemiology cannot answer with association alone This book keeps returning to two clinical questions, in different guises, from Chapter 2 onward. Do Cox-2 selective NSAIDs cause less peptic ulcer disease than nonselective NSAIDs? Do statins reduce the risk of a cardiovascular event when they are used the way clinicians actually use them, in routine care rather than in a trial? Both are causal questions, in that they ask what would happen to a group of patients if a particular treatment decision changed, and both are the kind of question epidemiologists are asked to answer using data collected for other purposes: medical records, claims, surveys, registries. The trouble is that the most natural thing to do with such data, namely compare patients who took a treatment to patients who did not, answers a different and easier question: whether patients who took the treatment did better or worse. Such a comparison yields an association. “Patients who took statins had fewer cardiovascular events” is a statement about a difference in outcomes between two groups of patients as they actually existed. “Statin initiation causes fewer cardiovascular events” is a statement about what would have happened to the same patients under a treatment decision they did not actually make. The two statements can point in the same direction, but nothing about them guarantees it, because the patients who took the treatment and the patients who did not usually differ in the first place, for reasons connected to their risk of the outcome. Two patterns of difference come up often enough in pharmacoepidemiology to have names. The first is the healthy-user effect: people who reliably take a preventive medication as prescribed also tend to exercise more, smoke less, keep other appointments, and generally do the many small things that predict good health, so a drug looks protective partly because the kind of person who takes it was already going to do well. Statins are a familiar example: some of the early apparent benefit of statin therapy in observational data reflected the fact that adherent, health-conscious patients are also less likely to have a heart attack for reasons unrelated to cholesterol. The second is confounding by indication, sometimes called channeling: physicians assign treatments according to their judgment of which patient needs them, so the treated group differs systematically in exactly the dimension the treatment is meant to address. A Cox-2 selective NSAID is often chosen, deliberately, for a patient a physician already suspects is at higher gastrointestinal risk, so that Cox-2 initiators can appear to fare worse with respect to peptic ulcer disease not because the drug fails to protect them but because they were a higher-risk group at baseline. If the direction of that confounding is misjudged, the apparent effect of a genuinely protective drug can be reversed. A third pattern worth naming here because it will recur throughout the book is prevalent-user bias: comparing people already on a treatment to people never treated mixes in everyone who started the drug, tolerated it, and stayed on it long enough to be captured in the data, while excluding the patients who stopped early because of side effects or lack of benefit. The comparisons in this book are built around new users — patients captured at the moment they start a drug, as ns and sta are — specifically to avoid folding that kind of survivorship into the treatment groups before the analysis begins. These concerns are not hypothetical. Observational studies of postmenopausal hormone therapy in the 1990s reported that use was associated with substantially lower risk of coronary heart disease; when the Women’s Health Initiative randomized women to hormone therapy or placebo, the trial found an increased risk. The discrepancy did not arise from careless analysis. Rather, women who used hormone therapy were healthier, more health-conscious, and more closely monitored than women who did not, a difference that simple adjustment did not fully remove. If a body of careful nonexperimental research can get the sign of an effect wrong, then a large or richly detailed data set is not by itself sufficient; what is needed is a framework that says when an association can be given a causal interpretation, and what to do when it cannot. The rest of the book develops such a framework. 1.2 A first look at the data We will spend the whole book with the two cohorts introduced properly in the next chapter, although it is worth looking at the simplest possible comparison in one of them now, before any adjustment, to see what an unadjusted answer to a causal question looks like. In ns, the cohort of new NSAID users, patients either initiated a nonselective NSAID or a Cox-2 selective inhibitor, and the outcome of interest is incident peptic ulcer disease (PUD). The crude risk of PUD in each group follows from a single group_by() and summarise(): risk_tab <- ns |> group_by(cox2_initiation) |> summarise(n = n(), risk = mean(pud)) risk_tab |> knitr::kable( col.names = c("Initiated drug", "N", "Risk of incident PUD"), digits = c(0, 0, 3) ) Initiated drug N Risk of incident PUD No 2642 0.098 Yes 240 0.125 Among the 2642 patients who initiated a nonselective NSAID, 9.8% went on to develop incident PUD; among the 240 patients who initiated a Cox-2 selective drug, the figure was 12.5%. Is that comparison an estimate of the causal effect of Cox-2 selectivity on peptic ulcer risk? It is not, and there is reason to think it is far from one. Nothing in the code above accounts for why a given patient started one drug rather than the other. Cox-2 selective inhibitors were developed, and are often chosen, specifically to reduce gastrointestinal risk in patients thought to need that protection. For example, a patient with a history of arthritis, prior GI bleeding, or concurrent corticosteroid or aspirin use is more likely to be steered toward the Cox-2 selective option. If Cox-2 initiators are systematically older or sicker in ways connected to ulcer risk, as we will confirm with a proper Table 1 in the next chapter, then the two rows of this table are not comparing like with like, and the crude risk difference above combines whatever causal effect the drug has with the baseline differences between the groups. Separating those two components, that is, asking what the comparison would look like if the two groups had been alike at baseline, is the problem the rest of the book addresses. 1.3 What this book covers The book is organized in four parts. Part I, Foundations, which this chapter opens, builds the conceptual vocabulary before any adjustment method is introduced: potential outcomes, the randomized trial as the benchmark against which a causal analysis is implicitly compared, causal diagrams for reasoning about which variables require adjustment, and the elements of study design that turn a causal question into an analyzable data set. Part II, Core Methods, covers the two families of tools most observational analyses reach for first: outcome regression and standardization, and propensity scores, culminating in inverse probability of treatment weighting. Part III, Time, Censoring, and Survival, brings in what happens when the outcome does not occur at a single fixed moment but can happen, or fail to happen, at any point over follow-up: survival analysis, censoring, inverse probability of censoring weights, and the clone-censor-weight approach to comparing dynamic treatment strategies, all worked out on the statin cohort, sta. Part IV, Beyond Exchangeability, deals with the harder case in which adjustment for measured covariates is insufficient because of unmeasured confounding, and introduces instrumental variables and sensitivity analysis as ways of asking what an unmeasured confounder would have to look like to explain away a finding. Threaded through all four parts is a toolkit that you will build yourself, one function at a time. By the end of the book you will have written, tested, and reused standardize() for outcome-model-based standardization, iptw_estimator() for propensity-score weighting, ipcw_estimator() for censoring weights, ccw_estimator() for the clone-censor-weight design, and iv_estimator() for instrumental variable analysis. Each is introduced once, in the chapter where its logic is developed, and then reused in a later exercise on the other cohort, with a different set of covariates, or with a different specification. Writing the functions yourself, rather than only calling a package’s implementation, is meant to make the assumptions each method depends on explicit. 1.4 How to read this book The chapters are meant to be read with R running alongside them. Every chapter is a self-contained R Markdown file that sources R/setup.R and rebuilds what it needs from there, so you can open any chapter, run it chunk by chunk, and confirm that the numbers in the text are the numbers the code produces. The two risks in the table above, for example, are computed from ns each time this chapter is rendered rather than typed in. When a new function is introduced, read the code closely enough to know what each argument does, then use it on data slightly different from the example in the text before moving to the exercises at the end of each chapter. The exercises themselves mostly do not ask you to write new methods; they ask you to point a function you already wrote at a different variable, a different cohort, or a different specification, and to think about whether the answer it gives still makes sense. That habit of applying a tool you understand to an unfamiliar problem is closer to what causal inference looks like in practice than anything else the book can offer.

Chapter 2 Getting started with R and the NAMCS data Every idea in this book is attached to code written in R. If you have never used R before, this chapter introduces enough of the tidyverse to read and write the data manipulations used in the chapters that follow, describes the two example cohorts we will work with for the rest of the semester, and ends by building a first reusable function: a “Table 1” generator that will be useful in most observational studies you conduct, in this course and after it. If you already know R and the tidyverse well, skim this chapter for the two data sets and read the Table 1 section, since table1_continuous() and table1_categorical() are used again in later chapters. 2.1 R, RStudio, and the tidyverse R is the language; RStudio is the editor most people use to write and run it. Appendix A walks through installing both, along with the packages this book relies on. Once they are installed, you will type or paste code into a script or, as here, into a code chunk inside an R Markdown document, and run it a line or a chunk at a time. The basic vocabulary of R is small. An object is a name that holds a value — a number, a piece of text, or, most often in this book, a rectangular data set with rows and columns (a data frame, or in the tidyverse a tibble). A function takes some input, does something to it, and returns an output; mean(x) takes a vector x and returns its average. A package is a bundle of functions someone else wrote and shared, loaded with library(). The tidyverse is one such bundle, or more precisely a collection of packages, including dplyr for manipulating data frames and ggplot2 for plotting, built around a shared design intended to make code read as a description of what you want done rather than as instructions for how a computer should do it. The setup chunk at the top of this chapter already did the loading for us: source("R/setup.R") runs a script that attaches the tidyverse, attaches the NAMCS package that supplies our example data, and builds the two analysis cohorts, ns and sta, that we will use throughout the book. Every chapter starts this way, so that it can be read and rendered on its own without depending on anything that came before it. The one piece of tidyverse syntax you should get comfortable with immediately is the pipe, |>. It takes whatever is on its left and passes it as the first argument to whatever is on its right, so that x |> f() means the same thing as f(x). This lets you chain several operations together and read them roughly left to right, top to bottom, as a sequence of steps: start with the data, then filter it, then summarize it. Four dplyr verbs will carry most of the weight in this book: filter() keeps rows that satisfy a condition, select() keeps particular columns, mutate() adds or changes a column, and group_by() paired with summarise() computes a statistic separately within each level of a grouping variable. A fifth, count(), is a shortcut for counting rows within groups. A few examples, all using the NSAID cohort ns: ns |> filter(age >= 65) |> nrow() ## [1] 501 ns |> select(cox2_initiation, age, sex) |> head(3) ## # A tibble: 3 × 3 ## cox2_initiation age sex ## <fct> <dbl> <chr> ## 1 No 44 Male ## 2 Yes 58 Female ## 3 No 78 Female ns |> mutate(age65 = as.integer(age >= 65)) |> count(age65) ## # A tibble: 2 × 2 ## age65 n ## <int> <int> ## 1 0 2381 ## 2 1 501 ns |> group_by(cox2_initiation) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age)) ## # A tibble: 2 × 3 ## cox2_initiation n mean_age ## <fct> <int> <dbl> ## 1 No 2642 47.3 ## 2 Yes 240 53.4 ns |> count(sex, cox2_initiation) ## # A tibble: 4 × 3 ## sex cox2_initiation n ## <chr> <fct> <int> ## 1 Female No 1552 ## 2 Female Yes 140 ## 3 Male No 1090 ## 4 Male Yes 100 The first line counts how many patients in ns are 65 or older. The second pulls out three columns and prints the first few rows. The third uses mutate() to add a new column, age65, that recodes age as a 0/1 indicator for being 65 or older, and then counts how many patients land in each category — the same recode-and-count pattern behind cox2_init and pud, the two convenience columns R/setup.R added for us. The fourth groups patients by which drug class they initiated and reports the number of patients and mean age in each group — a first, very small taste of the comparisons we will spend the rest of the book refining. The fifth cross-tabulates sex against treatment group. None of this is causal inference yet; it is description, but description is where an analysis begins, and it is worth being fluent in it before adding any causal machinery. 2.2 The NAMCS teaching cohorts The data behind every example in this book come from the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NAMCS), an annual survey of visits to office-based physicians in the United States. If you are ever unsure what a variable means, that is the place to check. 2.3 Plotting with ggplot2 ggplot2 builds a plot by mapping columns of data to visual properties — an x-axis, a y-axis, a color — and then adding layers on top that say how to draw it: as points, bars, lines, or histograms. Every ggplot2 call in this book starts the same way, with ggplot(data, aes(...)) naming the data and the mapping, followed by one or more geom_*() layers. A natural first question about ns is whether Cox-2 initiators and nonselective NSAID initiators look similar in age. A histogram, faceted by treatment group, answers this directly: ggplot(ns, aes(age)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0) + facet_wrap(~cox2_initiation) + labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Number of patients", title = "Age distribution by initiated drug class") Figure 2.1: Age distribution by initiated drug class. The two distributions are not identical, so age could confound any simple comparison of peptic ulcer risk between the groups, since age is plausibly related both to which drug a physician chooses to prescribe and to the baseline risk of peptic ulcer disease. A second question is whether the two groups differ in their burden of relevant comorbidities and comedications. A bar chart of prevalence, one bar per condition per group, is a compact way to see several comparisons at once: ns |> select(cox2_initiation, arthritis, diabetes, hypertension, corticosteroid_use) |> pivot_longer(-cox2_initiation, names_to = "condition") |> group_by(cox2_initiation, condition) |> summarise(prevalence = mean(value == "Yes"), .groups = "drop") |> ggplot(aes(condition, prevalence, fill = cox2_initiation)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Prevalence", fill = "Initiated Cox-2?") + coord_flip() Figure 2.2: Prevalence of selected comorbidities and comedications by initiated drug class. Arthritis, in particular, is more common among Cox-2 initiators than among nonselective NSAID initiators. This is clinically unsurprising, since Cox-2 selective drugs are often chosen for patients thought to be at higher gastrointestinal risk, and it is the kind of imbalance that will concern us once we take up adjustment for confounding. 2.4 Your first reusable functions: Table 1 Nearly every observational paper opens with a table comparing the characteristics of the groups under comparison, conventionally called “Table 1.” It is descriptive rather than causal, but it is where a reader first sees whether the groups appear comparable, and often where a reader first suspects that they are not. Because some version of this table is needed for nearly every study, we will write it once, as a function, and reuse it for the rest of the book. A function in R is defined with function(...), naming its arguments, followed by a body that computes something from them and returns it (by default, the value of the last expression evaluated). Writing your own functions will save a great deal of time, because it turns a block of code that would otherwise be copied, pasted, and slightly mis-edited into something written and tested once. A Table 1 needs to summarize two kinds of variables differently: continuous variables as a mean and standard deviation, and categorical variables as a count and percentage, both computed separately within each level of a grouping variable (here, treatment group). We will write one function for each. For continuous variables, the recipe is: reshape the requested columns into a long format with one row per patient per variable, group by the grouping variable and the variable name, compute "mean (sd)" as a formatted string, and reshape back so that each treatment group is its own column. table1_continuous <- function(data, vars, by) { data |> select(all_of(c(by, vars))) |> pivot_longer(all_of(vars), names_to = "variable") |> group_by(.data[[by]], variable) |> summarise( stat = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), sd(value, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop" ) |> pivot_wider(names_from = all_of(by), values_from = stat) } A couple of details are worth pointing out because they recur throughout this book. all_of(vars) tells select() and pivot_longer() that vars is a character vector of column names supplied by the caller, rather than a single column to look up literally, which is what allows the function to work for any set of variables rather than only the ones we happen to try first. .data[[by]] does the analogous thing for group_by(), letting the name of the grouping column be a string passed in as an argument rather than hard-coded. Together these are what make the function reusable: nothing about age or treatment group is written into the body of table1_continuous() itself. Categorical variables follow the same shape, but count levels instead of averaging values: table1_categorical <- function(data, vars, by) { data |> select(all_of(c(by, vars))) |> mutate(across(all_of(vars), as.character)) |> pivot_longer(all_of(vars), names_to = "variable", values_to = "level") |> count(.data[[by]], variable, level) |> group_by(.data[[by]], variable) |> mutate(stat = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n, 100 * n / sum(n))) |> ungroup() |> select(-n) |> pivot_wider(names_from = all_of(by), values_from = stat) } Both functions are saved in R/table1.R so that later chapters can pull them in with a single source() call rather than redefining them. Let’s use them on the NSAID cohort, comparing Cox-2 initiators to nonselective NSAID initiators on age and on five categorical covariates, and format the results with knitr::kable() for a readable table: source("R/table1.R") table1_continuous(ns, vars = "age", by = "cox2_initiation") |> knitr::kable() variable No Yes age 47.3 (16.6) 53.4 (15.7) table1_categorical( ns, vars = c("sex", "arthritis", "aspirin_use", "ppi_use", "corticosteroid_use"), by = "cox2_initiation" ) |> knitr::kable() variable level No Yes arthritis No 1849 (70.0%) 128 (53.3%) arthritis Yes 793 (30.0%) 112 (46.7%) aspirin_use No 2559 (96.9%) 231 (96.2%) aspirin_use Yes 83 (3.1%) 9 (3.8%) corticosteroid_use No 2629 (99.5%) 235 (97.9%) corticosteroid_use Yes 13 (0.5%) 5 (2.1%) ppi_use No 2562 (97.0%) 229 (95.4%) ppi_use Yes 80 (3.0%) 11 (4.6%) sex Female 1552 (58.7%) 140 (58.3%) sex Male 1090 (41.3%) 100 (41.7%) Look at the two tables side by side. Cox-2 initiators are, on average, older than nonselective NSAID initiators, and a substantially larger share of them have a history of arthritis. Neither table tells us whether Cox-2 selectivity affects peptic ulcer risk, a question that occupies the rest of the book, but both are the kind of descriptive evidence an epidemiologist examines first, and both came from two functions short enough to read line by line. 2.5 Exercises Build both a continuous and a categorical Table 1 for the statin cohort, comparing statin initiators to non-initiators (statin_use) on age and on diabetes, hypertension, and tobacco_use. Chapter 3 Potential outcomes and causal effects 3.1 Two futures for every patient 3.2 Simulating both potential outcomes 3.3 Average causal effects and estimands 3.4 The identification conditions 3.5 Exercises

Chapter 3 Potential outcomes and causal effects Chapter 1 asked whether Cox-2 selective NSAIDs cause less peptic ulcer disease than nonselective NSAIDs, and then showed that the obvious way of answering the question, comparing crude risks between the two groups, does not actually answer it, because Cox-2 initiators and nonselective initiators differ in ways connected to ulcer risk before either drug is ever taken. In this chapter we build the vocabulary needed to say precisely what went wrong in that comparison, and what an answer to the question would have to look like. The framework is called potential outcomes, and it allows a causal effect to be defined as a specific quantity that we can write down, simulate in code, and, under conditions we will state carefully, estimate from data. 3.1 Two futures for every patient Picture a single patient in the ns cohort — call her Patient 47 — who shows up at her physician’s office with joint pain that warrants an NSAID. Her physician has a choice: prescribe a nonselective NSAID, or prescribe a Cox-2 selective inhibitor. Whichever one is chosen, Patient 47 either does or does not go on to develop peptic ulcer disease over the following year. Although only one prescription is written, the question of what would have happened under the other still has a sensible answer. If she was in fact given the Cox-2 drug and stayed ulcer-free, we can ask coherently what would have happened to her, with everything else about her held fixed, had she instead received the nonselective drug. Potential outcomes provide notation for that question. Let \(A\) denote the treatment Patient 47 receives, coded \(A = 1\) for the Cox-2 selective drug and \(A = 0\) for the nonselective drug, and let \(Y\) denote whether she develops incident PUD. Then \(Y(1)\) is the outcome she would have if she were treated with \(A = 1\), and \(Y(0)\) is the outcome she would have if she were treated with \(A = 0\). These are potential outcomes, one for each treatment value she could in principle receive, and both are well-defined quantities before we know which treatment she actually gets. Once treatment is assigned, one of them becomes the observed outcome and the other becomes counterfactual: contrary to the fact of what happened. If Patient 47 actually receives the Cox-2 drug, we observe \(Y(1)\), and \(Y(0)\) is what her chart would show in the world where her physician wrote the other prescription. A note on notation is in order, since conventions differ across sources. We write these potential outcomes as \(Y(1)\) and \(Y(0)\), matching the PHS 921 lectures and exams, whereas many books, including Causal Inference: What If, use superscripts, \(Y^1\) and \(Y^0\) or \(Y^a\), and others write \(Y_a\) for the outcome under a generic treatment value \(a\). All three notations denote the same objects, and it is worth becoming comfortable moving between them rather than attaching the concept to any one of them. With both potential outcomes in hand for a single patient, her individual causal effect of Cox-2 selectivity on PUD is the contrast between them, \(Y(1) - Y(0)\). If \(Y(1) = 0\) and \(Y(0) = 1\), the Cox-2 drug prevented her ulcer; if both are 0, or both are 1, the choice of drug made no difference to her outcome, even though the drugs may differ substantially for other patients. Although this quantity is well defined, for any real patient it is unobservable. We only ever see one of Patient 47’s two potential outcomes, because she can only actually take one drug. This is what Holland (1986) called the fundamental problem of causal inference: for any individual, at most one potential outcome is ever realized, and the individual causal effect can never be computed from data on that individual alone, no matter how much we know about her or how long we follow her. Every method in this book is therefore a strategy for working around this problem. None of them recovers the missing potential outcome for any one patient; instead, they use groups of patients to estimate causal effects that are well defined on average, although they remain unknowable one person at a time. 3.2 Simulating both potential outcomes The fundamental problem of causal inference is a permanent limitation of real data: no data set on real patients ever contains both of anyone’s potential outcomes. In a simulated population, however, we are the ones writing the code, and so we decide both potential outcomes for every patient and can then observe what happens when only one of them is recorded. Such a simulation reproduces the causal question Chapter 1 raised, and it lets us watch confounding arise mechanically rather than merely describe it in words. Imagine 100,000 patients with a severity indicator, severity, that plays the role of an unmeasured driver of both treatment and outcome, capturing whatever led some patients toward the Cox-2 drug and also independently raised their ulcer risk. For each patient we generate both potential outcomes, y0 (the outcome under nonselective NSAID) and y1 (the outcome under Cox-2 selective drug), with the Cox-2 potential outcome built to carry a lower baseline risk, so that the drug is genuinely protective in this simulated world. We then assign actual treatment a so that more severe patients are more likely to receive the Cox-2 drug, which is the channeling Chapter 1 described, and construct the single outcome y actually recorded: the potential outcome matching the treatment each patient actually got. set.seed(921) truth <- tibble( severity = rbinom(100000, 1, 0.3), # confounder y0 = rbinom(100000, 1, 0.05 + 0.15 * severity), # risk untreated y1 = rbinom(100000, 1, 0.03 + 0.15 * severity), # risk treated a = rbinom(100000, 1, 0.2 + 0.5 * severity), # treated more if severe y = if_else(a == 1, y1, y0) # consistency ) truth |> summarise( ate = mean(y1) - mean(y0), att = mean(y1[a == 1]) - mean(y0[a == 1]), naive = mean(y[a == 1]) - mean(y[a == 0]) ) ## # A tibble: 1 × 3 ## ate att naive ## <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 -0.0202 -0.0237 0.0484 Because we generated y0 and y1 ourselves, we can compute the true average causal effect directly from columns no real data set would ever have both of at once: mean(y1) - mean(y0) is -0.020, a negative number, confirming that treatment is on average beneficial in this simulated population, lowering the risk of the outcome by about 2.0 percentage points. The last line of the summary, naive, is the only contrast we could ever compute from a real observational data set, being the mean of the observed outcome y among the treated minus the mean of y among the untreated, and it comes out to 0.048, positive and on the wrong side of zero. The naive comparison therefore suggests that Cox-2 selectivity is harmful, although we built the simulation so that it is beneficial. The gap between 0.048 and -0.020 is confounding by severity, visible here only because in this artificial world we know how the data were generated: severe patients were both more likely to be treated and more likely to have a bad outcome regardless of treatment, so the treated group looks worse than it would have if severity had been balanced across the two groups. Real data never provide y0 and y1 side by side, and the remainder of the chapter takes up the conditions under which the gap can nonetheless be closed. 3.3 Average causal effects and estimands The individual causal effect \(Y(1) - Y(0)\) cannot be observed, although its average over a population can be estimated once we have the right tools, which is why causal inference is framed in terms of population-level summaries called estimands. The one that shows up most often in this book is the average treatment effect (ATE), \[\text{ATE} = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)],\] the average, over everyone in the population of interest, of what would happen if everyone were treated minus what would happen if no one were. In the simulation above, mean(y1) - mean(y0) computed over all 100,000 patients is the ATE, because we happened to have both potential outcomes for every one of them. A second estimand, the average treatment effect in the treated (ATT), \[\text{ATT} = E[Y(1) \mid A = 1] - E[Y(0) \mid A = 1],\] restricts that same contrast to the patients who were actually treated: it asks what treatment did for the people who received it, not for the population as a whole. In the simulation, that is mean(y1[a == 1]) - mean(y0[a == 1]), and in our output it comes out very close to, but not exactly equal to, the ATE. That small remaining gap is Monte Carlo noise, not confounding: in this particular simulation the treatment effect y1 - y0 is built to be the same constant regardless of severity, so the true ATT equals the true ATE exactly, and the two only look different because both are estimated from a single finite sample of 100,000 patients rather than computed on the population itself. Rerunning with a different seed would shift the gap around, and often shrink it, without ever making it disappear completely. The two estimands diverge genuinely, rather than merely by chance, when the effect itself varies with whatever determines who gets treated. Which estimand is wanted then depends on the question being asked. If a health system is deciding whether to switch every future NSAID prescription for arthritis patients to the Cox-2 selective drug, the ATE is the relevant quantity, since it describes what would happen if everyone were treated. If a clinician is instead trying to understand the effect of the prescriptions she has already written, on the patients who actually received them, the ATT is closer to what she wants, since it describes whether that decision benefited the patients who received it. The two estimands coincide only when treatment effects do not vary with whatever determines who gets treated, which is the case built into this simulation; Exercise 3 asks you to relax that condition by making the effect depend on severity, so that the ATE and ATT genuinely differ. Any of these estimands can be reported on more than one scale. With \(Y\) binary, as PUD is, the most direct scale is the risk difference, \(E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]\), interpretable as “how many fewer (or more) cases per 100 patients treated.” The risk ratio, \(E[Y(1)] / E[Y(0)]\), expresses the same contrast multiplicatively, so that a risk ratio of 0.7 means treatment reduces risk by 30% regardless of baseline risk, which often makes it more portable across populations than a difference. The odds ratio, \[\frac{E[Y(1)]/(1-E[Y(1)])}{E[Y(0)]/(1-E[Y(0)])},\] is the scale most familiar from logistic regression and case-control studies, but it approximates the risk ratio only when the outcome is rare, and can otherwise diverge from it substantially. None of the identification conditions we turn to next, consistency, exchangeability, and positivity, depends on which scale is eventually reported. The choice of scale is a separate decision, made after identification, about how best to communicate a causal contrast. 3.4 The identification conditions Estimands like the ATE are defined in terms of potential outcomes we never fully observe. Identification is the step of showing that, under stated assumptions, an estimand written in potential outcomes is equal to some quantity we actually could compute from observed data. Three conditions do this work, and we state each one in terms of the NSAID cohort so that they read as claims about real patients. Consistency says that a patient’s observed outcome equals the potential outcome under the treatment she actually received: if Patient 47 takes the Cox-2 drug, her observed \(Y\) equals \(Y(1)\), not some average or blend involving \(Y(0)\). Although this sounds almost too obvious to state, it is doing real work, since it is what licenses the line y = if_else(a == 1, y1, y0) in the simulation above, and it can fail in practice when “treatment” is not well defined enough to pin down a single potential outcome. If “Cox-2 initiation” in fact bundles several different doses, durations, or concurrent gastroprotective strategies, then \(Y(1)\) refers to several distinct quantities rather than one, and consistency fails for reasons that have nothing to do with statistical estimation. Exchangeability (also called ignorability) says that the treated and untreated groups would have had the same average outcome had they received the same treatment — formally, \(Y(1), Y(0) \perp A\), potential outcomes are statistically independent of the treatment actually received. This is the condition that fails in our simulation: because a depends on severity, and severity also drives y0 and y1, treated and untreated patients are not exchangeable, which is why the naive contrast diverged from the ATE. A randomized trial delivers exchangeability by construction, as Chapter 4 makes precise, whereas confounding by indication removes it in observational data like ns, where physicians route sicker-looking patients toward the Cox-2 drug for reasons connected to the very outcome we are studying. Full exchangeability is usually too much to hope for in observational data, which is why most of this book works with a weaker version, conditional exchangeability: \(Y(1), Y(0) \perp A \mid L\) for some set of measured covariates \(L\). Treatment need not be independent of potential outcomes overall, only within levels of \(L\), so that among patients who share the same measured severity, say, treatment assignment is as good as random. This is a considerably more plausible assumption whenever we can measure the variables driving treatment choice, and it is the assumption that standardization, propensity scores, and IPTW in later chapters are built to exploit. Conditional exchangeability can be seen to work in our simulated example, since we have measured the one variable, severity, that was confounding the naive comparison. If we compute the same treated-minus-untreated contrast separately within each level of severity, using group_by(severity), we are conditioning on the confounder in the way conditional exchangeability requires: by_severity <- truth |> group_by(severity) |> summarise( naive_within = mean(y[a == 1]) - mean(y[a == 0]), .groups = "drop" ) by_severity ## # A tibble: 2 × 2 ## severity naive_within ## <int> <dbl> ## 1 0 -0.0184 ## 2 1 -0.0220 Within each level of severity, the treated-versus-untreated contrast comes out close to -0.020, the true ATE, rather than the badly biased 0.048 we obtained by ignoring severity altogether. Averaging these two severity-specific contrasts back together, weighted by how many patients fall in each severity stratum, recovers -0.019, essentially the ATE. The data themselves are unchanged; the only difference is that treated and untreated patients are now being compared within levels of the variable that was confounding the comparison. This hand-computed stratification is a simple case of standardization, which Chapter 7 develops into a general tool for covariate sets far too large to stratify by hand. Positivity (or overlap) says that every combination of covariates that occurs in the population has a nonzero probability of receiving either treatment level: \(0 < P(A = 1 \mid L = l) < 1\) for every value \(l\) of \(L\) with positive probability. Positivity is a logical precondition rather than a technical convenience. If every patient with severity == 1 in our simulation had probability zero of receiving the nonselective drug, there would be no untreated severe patients available for comparison, and no amount of adjustment could recover what their outcome under nonselective treatment would have been. Positivity can fail structurally, when a covariate combination makes one treatment clinically unthinkable, or only practically, when the combination is merely rare in a finite sample. The second, less absolute failure is common enough in real cohorts like ns that later chapters return to it when diagnosing propensity score overlap. Together, consistency, exchangeability (or its conditional version), and positivity are what let us write an equals sign between a causal estimand defined on unobservable potential outcomes and a statistical quantity computable from an observed data set like ns. The adjustment methods in the rest of this book, including standardization, propensity scores, and weighting, are different computational strategies for the same identified quantity, and none of them can substitute for these three conditions holding. 3.5 Exercises Modify the sim-po simulation so that the Cox-2 drug is harmful rather than beneficial — for instance, swap the coefficients so y1 has a higher baseline risk than y0 — and recompute the ATE, ATT, and naive contrast. Does the naive estimate still point in the wrong direction, and if so, which way? Starting from the original simulation, change how a is generated so that treatment no longer depends on severity at all (for example, rbinom(100000, 1, 0.4), a fixed probability for everyone). Recompute the three summary statistics. What happens to the gap between the naive contrast and the ATE, and why does that make sense in light of the exchangeability condition? Modify y1 so that the treatment effect itself differs by severity — for example, make the drug strongly protective for severe patients but do nothing for non-severe patients. Recompute the ATE and the ATT. Are they still close to each other? Relate what you find to the discussion of when ATE and ATT coincide, and to which estimand a clinician deciding whether to keep prescribing the drug to her current, already-treated patients should care about most.

Chapter 4 The randomized trial as the benchmark Chapter 3 named exchangeability as the condition that made the naive comparison in Chapter 1 fail: Cox-2 initiators and nonselective initiators were not exchangeable, because physicians routed patients toward one drug or the other based on characteristics connected to ulcer risk. That chapter also promised, in passing, that a randomized trial buys exchangeability “by construction,” rather than by an assumption you have to defend with subject-matter argument. In this chapter we make good on that promise, first in code and then in words, by showing why handing the treatment decision to a random number generator rather than to a physician’s judgment produces two groups that are, on average, alike with respect to both measured and unmeasured characteristics. We then consider what a randomized trial can and cannot still promise once patients stop doing what they were assigned to do, using the distinction between intention-to-treat and per-protocol analysis. Finally, we introduce the idea that organizes the rest of this book, the target trial, which is the discipline of writing down the trial one wishes one could run before attempting to emulate it with the data actually available. 4.1 Why randomization works Confounding by indication, as Chapter 1 described it, arises because treatment assignment is a function of patient characteristics connected to the outcome: a physician who suspects a patient is at elevated gastrointestinal risk is more likely to reach for the Cox-2 selective drug for exactly that patient, so Cox-2 initiators end up looking sicker on the very dimension the drug is meant to protect. Randomization addresses this at its source by making assignment a function of nothing about the patient at all, neither age nor arthritis history nor anything else a physician can observe, and, equally important, nothing a physician cannot observe. It is this last property that makes randomization more powerful than any adjustment strategy in this book. Matching, standardization, and propensity scores can balance only those covariates someone thought to measure, whereas a coin flip balances everything, including confounders no one ever recorded, because the assignment mechanism does not consult any characteristic of the patient, known or unknown. Formally, when \(A\) is generated by a physical randomization device rather than by clinical judgment, \(A\) is statistically independent of baseline covariates \(L\) and of both potential outcomes \(Y(1), Y(0)\) by the mechanics of assignment, so that the exchangeability condition from Chapter 3 is delivered as a feature of the design rather than assumed. We do not have an actual randomized trial of Cox-2 selectivity, only the ns cohort, in which treatment was a physician’s choice. We can, however, ask a narrower question of the data we do have: what would the Table 1 comparison and the crude risk comparison look like if the label “Cox-2 initiator” had been handed out by a coin flip instead of by a physician? mutate(a_rand = sample(cox2_init)) answers that question by shuffling which of the 2882 rows get called “1,” so that the same 240 Cox-2 labels in the data land on that many patients chosen completely at random, while every actual covariate and every actual outcome stays exactly as recorded. This is a relabeling exercise, not a new trial: nobody’s peptic ulcer disease status changes, because pud is not regenerated. The only thing the random draw decides is which of the real patients we call “arm 1” versus “arm 0” for the purpose of the comparison that follows. source("R/table1.R") table1_categorical( ns, vars = c("sex", "arthritis", "hypertension", "diabetes"), by = "cox2_init" ) |> knitr::kable( caption = "Table 1 under the real, physician-chosen assignment (0 = nonselective, 1 = Cox-2 selective)" ) Table 4.1: Table 1 under the real, physician-chosen assignment (0 = nonselective, 1 = Cox-2 selective) variable level 0 1 arthritis No 1849 (70.0%) 128 (53.3%) arthritis Yes 793 (30.0%) 112 (46.7%) diabetes No 2427 (91.9%) 209 (87.1%) diabetes Yes 215 (8.1%) 31 (12.9%) hypertension No 2037 (77.1%) 169 (70.4%) hypertension Yes 605 (22.9%) 71 (29.6%) sex Female 1552 (58.7%) 140 (58.3%) sex Male 1090 (41.3%) 100 (41.7%) set.seed(8) ns_rand <- ns |> mutate(a_rand = sample(cox2_init)) table1_categorical( ns_rand, vars = c("sex", "arthritis", "hypertension", "diabetes"), by = "a_rand" ) |> knitr::kable( caption = "Table 1 under the same patients, with the Cox-2 label reassigned by a coin flip (0/1 = random label)" ) Table 4.2: Table 1 under the same patients, with the Cox-2 label reassigned by a coin flip (0/1 = random label) variable level 0 1 arthritis No 1823 (69.0%) 154 (64.2%) arthritis Yes 819 (31.0%) 86 (35.8%) diabetes No 2416 (91.4%) 220 (91.7%) diabetes Yes 226 (8.6%) 20 (8.3%) hypertension No 2037 (77.1%) 169 (70.4%) hypertension Yes 605 (22.9%) 71 (29.6%) sex Female 1549 (58.6%) 143 (59.6%) sex Male 1093 (41.4%) 97 (40.4%) Look at arthritis first: under the real, physician-chosen assignment the gap between groups is 17 percentage points (46.7% among Cox-2 initiators versus 30.0% among nonselective initiators), which is large, and is the kind of systematic imbalance Chapter 2 already flagged when it introduced this Table 1. Under the randomly permuted label, the same comparison shrinks to 4.8 points. Diabetes behaves similarly: a real gap of 4.8 points falls to 0.2 under random assignment. Hypertension is an instructive exception, in that its gap under the random label happens to come out to 6.7 points, identical to the real gap of 6.7. Rather than indicating that hypertension remains confounded after randomization, this coincidence is a reminder that any single random split is only one draw among many possible draws, and that a single draw will not, by chance alone, look perfectly balanced on every variable. What randomization guarantees is that mismatches of this kind are unsystematic: if we rerun the shuffle with a different seed, the hypertension coincidence disappears, while arthritis and diabetes continue to come back close to balanced, since approximate balance is what randomization delivers on average rather than in any particular draw. The same logic applies to the outcome itself. Because pud was never regenerated, the treated and untreated groups defined by a_rand are being compared on outcomes that already happened, for reasons that had nothing to do with a_rand. contrasts <- bind_rows( ns |> summarise( assignment = "real (cox2_init)", risk_0 = mean(pud[cox2_init == 0]), risk_1 = mean(pud[cox2_init == 1]) ), ns_rand |> summarise( assignment = "randomly permuted (a_rand)", risk_0 = mean(pud[a_rand == 0]), risk_1 = mean(pud[a_rand == 1]) ) ) |> mutate(diff = risk_1 - risk_0) contrasts |> knitr::kable(digits = 4) assignment risk_0 risk_1 diff real (cox2_init) 0.0977 0.125 0.0273 randomly permuted (a_rand) 0.0999 0.100 0.0001 The real crude contrast reproduces Chapter 1’s finding: Cox-2 initiators have a 2.7-point higher crude risk of PUD than nonselective initiators, the wrong-signed, confounded comparison this whole book exists to fix. The randomly permuted contrast, computed from the identical set of recorded pud values, comes out to 0.01 points, which is indistinguishable from zero. No patient’s actual outcome changed between the two rows of that table; the only difference is which label we used to split the data into two groups. When the label carries no information about who received it, as a coin flip guarantees, the crude contrast is an unbiased estimate of a null effect, and it recovers one. When the label is instead a physician’s judgment, correlated with everything that judgment was trying to account for, the same arithmetic turns up a gap that has nothing to do with the drug. This is why the randomized trial is described as the benchmark. The reason is not that any one trial is guaranteed a perfectly matched Table 1, since chance imbalance of the sort seen for hypertension above does occur, but rather that whatever mismatch remains is due to chance alone, which is the kind of uncertainty that ordinary confidence intervals are built to quantify. Confounding by indication is a different kind of error, and no amount of additional data makes it smaller, because it is not noise. Every design and every adjustment method in the rest of this book is judged by how close it comes to the null contrast that randomization produced in this section without any adjustment at all. 4.2 Intention-to-treat and per-protocol A coin flip decides the arm a patient is assigned to; it does not decide what that patient actually does afterward. In a real Cox-2 trial, some patients randomized to the Cox-2 arm would stop the drug early because of side effects or cost, some randomized to nonselective NSAIDs would switch to Cox-2 therapy if their joint pain persisted, and some in either arm would take over-the-counter NSAIDs the protocol never intended to capture. Once assignment and actual treatment can diverge, a trial supports (at least) two different analyses, and they answer two different questions. The intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis compares patients according to the arm they were randomized to, regardless of what treatment they actually went on to receive. Writing \(A\) for randomized assignment, the ITT contrast is \(E[Y \mid A = 1] - E[Y \mid A = 0]\), computed on the groups the randomization device itself created. Because \(A\) is here the coin flip, ITT preserves exchangeability as constructed, and the comparison remains a contrast between groups that differ, on average, only by that coin flip, however much nonadherence occurs afterward. For this reason ITT is the default primary analysis in nearly every large randomized trial, being the one contrast that inherits randomization’s guarantee without further qualification. That guarantee, however, comes at a cost of interpretation, because ITT does not estimate the effect of taking the assigned drug. It estimates the effect of being assigned to a strategy, which is a blend of the effect among patients who followed it and the effect among patients who did not. When nonadherence is common, ITT effects are typically attenuated toward the null relative to the effect of full adherence, so that a drug that would be beneficial if everyone took it as directed can produce a modest or null ITT result if enough assigned patients discontinue treatment. The per-protocol analysis attempts to recover the more specific question by restricting to, or reclassifying patients according to, what they actually did, comparing adherers to the Cox-2 strategy against adherers to the nonselective strategy rather than comparing the arms as randomized. Although this is often the clinically more interesting question, once patients are grouped by what they actually did rather than by what the coin flip assigned them, the randomization at baseline no longer protects the comparison. Whatever led a given patient to adhere rather than switch or discontinue (eg, symptom severity, general health, health literacy, or tolerance of side effects) may also be connected to the outcome, which is the mechanism Chapter 1 called the healthy-user effect, now operating inside a randomized trial rather than across an observational cohort. A naive per-protocol comparison can therefore be confounded even though the trial that produced the data was, at the point of randomization, perfectly randomized. The sta cohort makes these concerns concrete without requiring a real trial. Because sta is observational, and nobody was randomized to start a statin, any comparison of patients who initiated and stayed on a statin for some minimum duration against everyone else is already per-protocol in spirit, and already vulnerable to the same self-selection just described. It is vulnerable to a further problem as well: misclassifying the follow-up time before a patient meets the “adherer” criterion can build survival into the definition of one of the groups, a distortion called immortal time bias that Chapter 6 introduces on its own terms. Chapter 12 develops the clone-censor-weight approach specifically to answer a per-protocol-style question — what would happen if patients followed a specific treatment strategy for its full duration — using observational data like sta, without letting either kind of bias back in. 4.3 The target trial Every method in this book adjusts observational data so that it can stand in for a randomized trial. Hernán and Robins (2016) turned that observation into a discipline, called the target trial framework: for any causal question one wants to answer with observational data, one first specifies, in full protocol detail, the randomized trial that would answer it, as though funding, ethics, and recruitment were not obstacles, and only then describes how each piece of that protocol will be emulated using the data actually available. Almost none of the trials specified this way will ever be run. The value of writing the protocol anyway is that it brings every design decision a trial would have to make (who is eligible, what counts as each treatment strategy, when follow-up starts, and how the outcome is defined) into the open before any adjustment method is chosen, instead of leaving those decisions implicit in a modeling script. Here is that protocol, written out for the Cox-2 question this book has been asking since Chapter 1: Protocol component Target trial Emulation using ns Eligibility Adults beginning NSAID therapy, with no NSAID use in the preceding period Same criterion, applied when ns was assembled: new users only Treatment strategies (1) Initiate a Cox-2 selective NSAID; (2) initiate a nonselective NSAID cox2_init == 1 versus cox2_init == 0 at the qualifying prescription Assignment Random allocation to strategy (1) or (2) Not randomized; approximated by conditioning on measured confounders (ns_covs) under the conditional exchangeability assumption from Chapter 3 Follow-up Begins at randomization (“time zero”) and continues to the outcome, loss to follow-up, or a fixed administrative end Begins at the qualifying prescription date, ends at incident PUD, loss to follow-up, or the administrative end Outcome Incident peptic ulcer disease pud == 1 observed during follow-up Causal contrast Intention-to-treat comparison of the two assigned strategies ITT analog: compare all patients who initiated each strategy at time zero, regardless of later switching or discontinuation Analysis plan Risk difference or risk ratio between arms, estimated directly from randomized groups Same contrast, estimated with an adjustment method (standardization, propensity scores, or IPTW — Chapters 7 through 9) that stands in for randomization Six of these seven rows can already be written down for ns with no controversy, in the same language a trial protocol would use: the eligibility criteria are those used to identify new users, the two strategies are already coded in cox2_init, follow-up already has a defined start and end, the outcome is already defined as pud, and even the causal contrast and analysis plan can be stated without needing to resolve anything about confounding first. Only the Assignment row cannot be filled in as “randomized,” because assignment was not randomized, and that single row is where the rest of this book does its work. Standardization and outcome regression, propensity scores and inverse probability weighting, and instrumental variables and sensitivity analysis are each a different technical strategy for filling in that one row with something that behaves enough like a coin flip to make the causal contrast in the last row credible. Chapters 6, 10, and 12 return to a version of this same protocol, adapted for study design choices, for survival outcomes, and for the dynamic treatment strategies studied in sta, although the structure of the argument is the same in each case: specify the trial first, then argue, row by row, for how well the observational data emulate it. One application of this logic has become common enough in regulatory submissions to deserve a name here. In an external control arm design, a single-arm trial — typically in a rare disease, or in an oncology setting where randomizing patients to the standard of care is hard to justify — is compared against a comparator group assembled from observational data: a disease registry, an electronic health record extract, or the control arm of an earlier trial. The target trial is the two-arm randomized trial that was not run, and the emulation problem is the one Part II of this book spends its chapters on, since the trial patients and the external controls were selected by different criteria, treated in different calendar periods, and followed by different means. Every row of the protocol table therefore has to be argued for rather than assumed, and the Assignment row carries the same weight it carries above, which is why the confounding machinery of the next several chapters applies here without alteration. The course’s session on external control arms works through examples of submissions that were accepted and of submissions that were not. 4.4 Exercises Draft a target trial protocol table, in the same seven-row format used above, for the statin question this book has been asking alongside the Cox-2 question. Use the sta cohort and sta_covs to fill in eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment, follow-up, outcome, causal contrast, and analysis plan in your own words. Immortal time bias was named in this chapter as a hazard for per-protocol-style comparisons in sta, and Chapter 6 takes it up in full. Looking at the seven rows of the target trial table above, which single protocol component does immortal time bias violate, and why does misclassifying a patient’s follow-up before they meet a treatment-defining criterion break that component specifically, rather than, say, the eligibility or outcome rows?

Chapter 5 Causal diagrams Chapter 1 named confounding by indication in words: physicians steer Cox-2 selective NSAIDs toward patients they already judge to be at higher gastrointestinal risk, which is why the crude comparison came out backwards. Chapter 3 gave that idea a formal home inside potential outcomes, as a failure of exchangeability, and named the covariates that would need to be equal on average across treatment groups for a comparison to be believable. Neither chapter offered a way to look at a causal assumption and read off which variables belong on that list, or, equally important, which variables do not belong on it and would damage the analysis if included. In this chapter we develop that language. A causal diagram translates a set of substantive beliefs about how variables relate to one another into a picture that can be reasoned about with a small number of rules, checked with software, and reviewed by colleagues who may not share our subject-matter expertise but can still read a graph. 5.1 Drawing causal assumptions A causal diagram, in the sense we use throughout this book, is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): a collection of nodes, one for each variable that matters to the question, connected by arrows that represent direct causal effects. An arrow from \(A\) to \(B\) asserts that \(A\) has some effect on \(B\), holding everything else in the picture fixed; the absence of an arrow is an equally substantive claim, that no such direct effect exists. “Acyclic” rules out feedback loops drawn as a single static picture, so that \(A\) cannot cause \(B\) which causes \(A\) within the same diagram, although time can be represented by drawing \(A\) at one point in time and \(A\) at a later point as two separate nodes. Every arrow in a DAG represents a claim that someone is prepared to defend on scientific grounds, rather than a quantity estimated from data, and the diagram is where such assumptions are written down and debated before any model is fit. A path between two nodes is any sequence of arrows connecting them, regardless of direction. Some paths are causal paths: every arrow along the way points forward, from the exposure toward the outcome, tracing an actual mechanism by which the exposure could affect the outcome. Other paths are backdoor paths: they connect exposure to outcome but enter the exposure node through an arrow pointing into it, meaning they trace a route through some third variable that causes both, rather than an effect of the exposure itself. A crude comparison of exposed and unexposed patients pools every open path between them, causal and backdoor alike, which is why Chapter 1’s comparison of Cox-2 initiators and nonselective initiators mixed whatever real effect Cox-2 selectivity has on ulcer risk with whatever backdoor paths ran through GI risk, age, and steroid use. The goal of adjustment, translated into this graphical language, is to close every backdoor path while leaving every causal path open. This criterion is precise enough that software can check it, as the next section demonstrates for the NSAID question. The formal name for the state we are aiming at is d-separation: two variables are d-separated, given a set of conditioning variables, when every path between them is blocked. It is the term used in the course’s DAG workshop and throughout the graphical-models literature, and it is what dagitty is checking when we ask it whether an adjustment set suffices. 5.2 The NSAID–PUD diagram We now encode in a diagram the causal story Chapters 1 and 3 have been telling about Cox-2 selectivity and peptic ulcer disease: GI risk factors, age, and corticosteroid use each influence a physician’s choice between a Cox-2 selective and a nonselective NSAID, and each also influences ulcer risk directly, alongside whatever effect the drug itself has. library(ggdag) dag_nsaid <- dagify( pud ~ cox2 + gi_risk + age + steroids, cox2 ~ gi_risk + age + steroids, exposure = "cox2", outcome = "pud", labels = c(cox2 = "Cox-2 selective", pud = "Peptic ulcer", gi_risk = "GI risk factors", age = "Age", steroids = "Corticosteroids") ) ggdag(dag_nsaid, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") + theme_dag() The diagram makes the confounding structure explicit: gi_risk, age, and steroids each sit upstream of both cox2 and pud, so each one opens a backdoor path from cox2 to pud that has nothing to do with the drug’s own effect — cox2 <- gi_risk -> pud, cox2 <- age -> pud, and cox2 <- steroids -> pud, alongside the single causal path cox2 -> pud that is the object of interest. Rather than reason through each backdoor path by hand, we can let dagitty do it directly: dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag_nsaid) ## { age, gi_risk, steroids } adjustmentSets() reports a single minimal set here: {age, gi_risk, steroids}. That result tells us two things. First, adjusting for all three variables together closes every backdoor path in the diagram, so that a comparison of Cox-2 and nonselective initiators that conditions on age, GI risk factors, and steroid use, whether by stratification, standardization, or a propensity score built from them (the subjects of Chapters 7 through 9), is no longer contaminated by the confounding this diagram encodes. Second, no smaller set will suffice: because each of the three variables opens its own separate backdoor path with no shared intermediate node, dropping any one of them leaves that path open, and the comparison remains confounded through whichever variable was left out. This is the graphical counterpart of the conditional exchangeability condition from Chapter 3, \(Y(a) \perp A \mid L\) for \(L\) equal to this adjustment set, with the difference that the set is here read off a picture rather than asserted, and that the diagram remains available for a colleague to challenge by redrawing an arrow. 5.3 Confounders, colliders, and mediators Real diagrams can have dozens of nodes, although nearly everything about how adjustment behaves follows from three small structures that recur throughout them. Recognizing each structure, and adjusting only for the first of the three, accounts for most of what this chapter is meant to teach. A confounder is a common cause of exposure and outcome, the pattern gi_risk, age, and steroids all instantiate above: a variable with arrows pointing into both the exposure and the outcome, opening a backdoor path that adjustment is meant to close. dag_confounder <- dagify( y ~ x + c, x ~ c, exposure = "x", outcome = "y", labels = c(x = "Exposure", y = "Outcome", c = "Confounder") ) ggdag(dag_confounder, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") + theme_dag() A collider is the mirror image: a common effect of two other variables, with arrows pointing into it from both sides rather than out of it. dag_collider <- dagify( m ~ x + z, exposure = "x", outcome = "z", labels = c(x = "Cause 1", z = "Cause 2", m = "Collider") ) ggdag(dag_collider, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") + theme_dag() Left alone, a collider does nothing to the association between its two causes, so that if x and z are independent they remain independent whether or not anyone ever looks at m. Difficulties arise once m is conditioned on, whether deliberately, by restricting a sample to m’s observed value, or inadvertently, by studying only the patients who survived to be observed at all. Conditioning on a common effect induces an association between its causes where none existed, because within any fixed value of m, learning that one cause was small makes the other cause more likely to have been large enough to produce that value of m on its own. We can make this concrete with a short simulation, in which we draw two variables that are causally unrelated to each other, build a third variable as their common effect, and compare the association between the first two before and after restricting to one level of the third. set.seed(5) n <- 5000 gi_risk_indep <- rnorm(n) # cause 1, unrelated to cause 2 by construction frailty <- rnorm(n) # cause 2, unrelated to cause 1 by construction # collider: a variable such as "hospitalized" driven by both causes plus noise hosp_score <- gi_risk_indep + frailty + rnorm(n) hospitalized <- as.integer(hosp_score > quantile(hosp_score, 0.75)) collider_df <- tibble(gi_risk_indep, frailty, hospitalized) fit_full <- lm(frailty ~ gi_risk_indep, data = collider_df) fit_cond <- lm(frailty ~ gi_risk_indep, data = collider_df |> filter(hospitalized == 1)) We simulated gi_risk_indep and frailty as independent draws, so the true association between them is zero by construction, and the regression run on the full sample confirms it: the slope is 0.014 (p = 0.34), indistinguishable from no relationship at all. When we restrict that same regression to the 1250 patients in the top quartile of the collider score — patients who were “hospitalized” in this simulation — we turn that null slope into -0.306 (p < 0.001), a strong and highly significant association between two variables that have no causal connection at all. Nothing about the data-generating process differs between the two regressions; only the sample does. This is collider bias, and it illustrates that adjustment applied to the wrong kind of node does not merely fail to help but induces the sort of spurious association that the methods in this book are intended to avoid. The third structure is a mediator: a variable that sits on the causal path itself, transmitting some or all of the exposure’s effect on the way to the outcome rather than confounding it. dag_mediator <- dagify( y ~ m, m ~ x, exposure = "x", outcome = "y", labels = c(x = "Exposure", m = "Mediator", y = "Outcome") ) ggdag(dag_mediator, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") + theme_dag() Adjusting for a mediator is a different error from adjusting for a collider, since a mediator is genuinely caused by the exposure and genuinely causes the outcome, although it remains inappropriate for the question we ask throughout this book, which concerns the total effect of exposure on outcome. Conditioning on m blocks the causal path x -> m -> y that carries the effect we are trying to estimate, so a regression of y on x that also includes m answers a narrower question, namely how much of the effect operates independently of that pathway, while resembling the same kind of adjusted analysis that closes a backdoor path. Confounders therefore belong in the adjustment set, whereas colliders and mediators, for their different reasons, do not. 5.4 Selection bias as collider stratification The collider simulation above used “hospitalized” as a placeholder, although the same mechanism underlies a problem known by a more familiar name, selection bias. The structural reading of selection bias, in which it is understood as conditioning on a collider rather than as a catalog of study-design mishaps, is the account given by Hernán, Hernández-Díaz, and Robins (2004), and it is the one the rest of this section follows. Suppose Cox-2 selectivity has some effect on the chance a patient tolerates therapy long enough to stay in a study, and, independently, that some unmeasured element of a patient’s underlying prognosis also affects whether they remain in follow-up long enough to have their outcome observed. “Remained in the study” is then a collider, with an arrow into it from treatment and an arrow into it from unmeasured prognosis. dag_selection <- dagify( pud ~ u, s ~ cox2 + u, exposure = "cox2", outcome = "pud", labels = c(cox2 = "Cox-2 selective", pud = "Peptic ulcer", u = "Unmeasured prognosis", s = "Remained in study") ) ggdag(dag_selection, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") + theme_dag() Any analysis that sees only patients who remained in the study, which describes every complete-case analysis unless something deliberate is done about it, is conditioning on s whether or not a filter() call was ever written, because patients who were lost to follow-up do not appear in the rows being summed. By the same logic as the simulation above, that conditioning can open an association between cox2 and pud running through u, even in a world where the diagram already grants that GI risk, age, and steroid use have been fully adjusted for and the drug has no effect on ulcer risk. Measuring additional baseline covariates does not remove this bias, since it does not arise from confounding but from which patients are present to be analyzed at all, after treatment has had a chance to influence who stays and who leaves. Chapter 11 takes up this problem under its clinical name, informative censoring, and develops inverse probability of censoring weights, which reweight the patients who remain so that they stand in, on average, for everyone who should have been followed. 5.5 Exercises Add a node for otc_nsaid (over-the-counter NSAID use, unmeasured in ns) to dag_nsaid, with arrows into both cox2 and pud, and re-run dagitty::adjustmentSets() on the result. Does an adjustment set still exist? If otc_nsaid cannot be included because it is never recorded, what does that imply about the conditional exchangeability assumption from Chapter 3 as applied to the ns cohort? Explain, in terms of the collider mechanism, why conditioning on either tail of a common effect induces an association, while conditioning on nothing (the full sample) does not. Consider a study of SSRI use and lung cancer. Coronary artery disease is the variable of the four most reliably recorded in claims data, so an analyst who could adjust for only one thing would be tempted by it. Then run adjustmentSets() on your diagram and report the minimal sufficient set.
