Chapter 6 Study design for causal questions Chapter 3 introduced estimands, Chapter 4 developed the target trial as the protocol against which any observational analysis is implicitly compared, and Chapter 5 showed how a confounding structure can be read off a diagram. Each of those chapters, however, assumed that the rows of the target trial table — who is eligible, what counts as each treatment strategy, when follow-up starts — had already been settled before any adjustment method entered the picture. In this chapter we take up those decisions. We consider three design choices that determine what a causal comparison is capable of estimating, independent of which model eventually gets fit to the data: choosing new users over prevalent users, choosing an active comparator over no treatment at all, and aligning the moment a patient becomes eligible with the moment their follow-up clock starts. If any of the three is specified badly, no amount of standardization, propensity-score weighting, or careful modeling in the chapters ahead will repair it, because the bias has entered through which rows and which person-time were analyzed. 6.1 Design before analysis An estimand, in the language of Chapter 3, is a contrast between potential outcomes in some population — the ATE if we mean everyone, the ATT if we mean the patients who were actually treated. Which contrast we can identify from a data set is decided well before any regression is fit, by choices that belong entirely to design: who is eligible to enter the cohort, what distinguishes the treatment groups, when each patient’s clock starts, and which group the treated patients are measured against. The target trial protocol of Chapter 4 is essentially a checklist of these decisions, written out in the same seven rows a trial’s own protocol would use, and it is deliberately silent on adjustment: eligibility, treatment strategies, and follow-up can all be specified in full before standardization or weighting is mentioned. That ordering matters because no statistical method can repair a design that answers the wrong question. If eligibility quietly mixes patients who have been on a drug for years with patients just starting it, the sample no longer corresponds to any one estimand — neither the effect of starting the drug nor the effect of continuing it — no matter how well the eventual model fits. Standardization, propensity scores, and inverse probability weighting, the subjects of Part II, are strategies for closing a measured gap in exchangeability once the design has fixed which patients are being compared and at what moment; they cannot rescue a design that never posed an answerable question. This chapter works through three of the design decisions most responsible for that failure in pharmacoepidemiology, and shows how each is already built into the two cohorts we have used since Chapter 1. 6.2 New-user designs Chapter 1 mentioned prevalent-user bias in passing. Here we consider why it distorts a comparison and how a new-user design addresses it. A prevalent-user comparison enrolls patients who are already on a drug, of whatever duration, and compares them to patients who are not. Two distinct problems follow from that choice, although they usually occur together. The first is depletion of susceptibles: patients who could not tolerate a drug, or for whom it plainly was not working, tend to stop taking it early and so drop out of the pool of “current users” long before anyone samples that pool. The current users who remain are enriched with patients who tolerated the drug well, which biases any comparison toward the drug appearing safer and more effective than it is for the population that ever started it. The second problem is that covariates measured at the same moment as prevalent exposure may already have been changed by the treatment itself. A blood pressure reading taken after several years on a drug reflects, in part, whatever the drug did to blood pressure; using it to “adjust for confounding” adjusts away part of the treatment effect, or, if some other unmeasured factor drives both that downstream covariate and the outcome, opens the kind of collider path Chapter 5 warned against. The new-user design avoids both problems by anchoring the cohort to the moment of treatment initiation rather than to some arbitrary later moment of observation. A patient enters the cohort only when we observe them starting the drug, with no recorded use of that drug or its class immediately beforehand, and every covariate used for adjustment is measured at or before that same moment — before treatment has had any chance to change it. This is how ns was built. Among NAMCS office visits from 2005 through 2009, a patient enters ns at the visit at which they are observed initiating an NSAID, with no current NSAID use recorded at that visit, and their initiating prescription — Cox-2 selective or nonselective — fixes which arm, cox2_initiation, they belong to for the rest of the cohort. Of the 2882 patients in ns, 240 are captured this way as Cox-2 initiators and the rest as nonselective initiators; nobody in either group had already been taking an NSAID before the qualifying visit, and nobody’s baseline covariates were measured after the drug had a chance to act on them. ns is therefore already a new-user cohort by construction, although we had not previously named the design principle it follows. The idea generalizes beyond initiation. Starting a drug is one clinical decision, but stopping one, switching, and intensifying a dose are decisions too, and each can anchor a comparison in the same way: enroll patients at the moment the decision is made, classify them by what was decided, and follow them forward. This framing — the treatment decision design (Brookhart 2015) — is the general form of the new-user design, and it is what allows the target trials of Chapter 4 to be emulated at decision points other than a first prescription; Chapter 12’s treatment strategies rest on this view. Pharmacoepidemiology has accumulated names for the specific ways these comparisons go wrong, and the names are worth knowing because they are how reviewers will describe your study. Each is a special case of confounding or of misaligned time, and each is addressed by some part of the new-user, active-comparator design. Healthy user effect. Patients who start and continue a preventive therapy also tend to exercise, undergo screening, and follow other medical advice, so an apparent benefit of the drug may instead reflect the behavior of the patients taking it (Chapter 1). An active comparator mitigates this, since patients in both arms have consulted a physician and accepted a prescription. Healthy adherer effect. The same phenomenon operating within a trial or a cohort arm: because adherence is itself a marker of health, a comparison of adherent with nonadherent patients confounds the effect of the drug with the disposition of the patients who take it. Design alone does not address this; the protocol weights of Chapter 12 do. Sick stopper effect. Patients who become ill tend to discontinue treatment, so untreated person-time becomes enriched with patients who are about to experience outcomes. Following new users from a fixed time zero keeps discontinuation downstream of the exposure assignment rather than letting it redefine that assignment. Protopathic bias. A drug prescribed for the earliest symptoms of an as-yet-undiagnosed disease will appear to cause the disease it was intended to treat. Anchoring time zero at initiation, and where necessary lagging the outcome window, keeps the drug from being blamed for the condition that prompted the prescription. Depletion of susceptibles. Described above: prevalent users are those who survived the early attrition, so the pool is enriched with patients who tolerate the drug. Enrolling patients at initiation instead samples everyone who ever started. 6.3 Active-comparator designs A new-user design still leaves open a further choice: new users of the drug of interest, compared to what? The most obvious comparator is patients who did not start any NSAID at all, although for this question that is a poor choice. Whether a physician prescribes an NSAID in the first place is itself a treatment decision, driven by whether a patient has arthritis, joint pain, or another condition that calls for one — and that same decision is entangled with everything connected to needing an NSAID at all, most of which has nothing to do with GI risk specifically. Comparing Cox-2 initiators to non-initiators folds confounding by indication for needing an NSAID together with whatever separately drives the choice between the two drug classes, and the resulting mixture is much harder to reason about than either piece alone. An active-comparator design removes the first of these by drawing the comparison group from patients who also started an NSAID, of the other class. Every patient in ns, regardless of arm, already needed and received NSAID therapy, so whatever led a physician to prescribe an NSAID in the first place is held approximately fixed across both arms and cannot by itself produce imbalance between them. What can still differ between Cox-2 initiators and nonselective initiators is the narrower set of factors that lead a physician to prefer one NSAID over the other once the decision to prescribe an NSAID has been made: age, history of GI risk, and concurrent steroid use, which is the adjustment set {age, gi_risk, steroids} identified by Chapter 5’s DAG. An active comparator does not eliminate confounding. It narrows the set of variables we have to worry about from everything connected to needing pain treatment down to whatever distinguishes one NSAID from the other, a set that is more plausibly measured in full and more amenable to the adjustment methods of Part II. We can see how much confounding remains, and along which covariates, by rebuilding Chapter 2’s Table 1 for every covariate in ns_covs rather than the handful used there for illustration. ns_covs mixes The gaps that do map onto the diagram — arthritis and the conditions that accompany it, age, and corticosteroid use — are the ones that Part II’s adjustment methods are meant to close. 6.4 Immortal time and other time-zero problems A design can specify eligibility and the comparator correctly and still fail on a third dimension: when each patient’s follow-up clock starts. Aligned time zero means that three things happen on the same date for every patient: the date they are confirmed eligible, the date they are classified into a treatment strategy, and the date their person-time starts counting toward the outcome. ns satisfies this automatically, because eligibility, drug class, and the start of follow-up are all pinned to the same qualifying visit. The requirement is easy to state, but it is violated whenever a study defines “exposed” using information that could only be known after follow-up had already begun. A worked hypothetical shows how the violation operates. It is built around a definition of treatment that is common in pharmacoepidemiology: a patient is called a “user” only once a second prescription has been filled, some grace period after the first. Suppose we simulate 20,000 hypothetical patients, each with a true time to death that is, by construction, unrelated to anything about their future drug-taking behavior, and suppose “persistent user” status requires two things: surviving past a 90-day grace period, and an independent adherence habit that is fixed for each patient and has no effect on survival. set.seed(6) n <- 20000 grace <- 90 follow_up <- 730 hyp <- tibble( id = 1:n, death_time = rexp(n, rate = 1 / 2000), adherent = rbinom(n, 1, 0.6) # a habit unrelated to survival, by construction ) |> mutate( alive_grace = death_time > grace, persistent = as.integer(alive_grace & adherent == 1), died_by_end = as.integer(death_time <= follow_up) ) A naive analysis, of the kind a misaligned time zero produces, starts every patient’s clock on day zero and compares mortality risk between “persistent users” and everyone else over the full 730-day window: naive_tab <- hyp |> group_by(persistent) |> summarise(n = n(), risk = mean(died_by_end), .groups = "drop") naive_tab |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) persistent n risk 0 8538 0.349 1 11462 0.276 Persistent users appear strongly protected, with mortality risk 7.3 percentage points lower than everyone else, even though adherence was given no causal effect on survival in the simulation. The explanation is mechanical rather than clinical. To be labeled “persistent,” a patient had to survive at least 90 days, so the persistent group begins its 730-day follow-up with 90 days during which a death could not have occurred, whatever the composition of that group. This guaranteed event-free interval is immortal time, and it arises entirely because the exposure definition depends on information — survival through the grace period — that was not available at the true time zero, the date treatment actually started. The remedy is to give every patient the same time zero regardless of group, restricting the comparison to patients who survived to the end of the grace period and starting follow-up at day 90 rather than at day zero. landmark_tab |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) adherent n risk 0 7668 0.275 1 11462 0.276 Among the 19130 patients who survived to day 90, adherent and non-adherent patients now have essentially identical mortality risk over the remaining follow-up (0.276 versus 0.275, a difference of 0.001) — indistinguishable from the null effect we built into the simulation. Nothing about any patient differed between the two analyses. Only the point at which follow-up was allowed to begin changed, and that change alone was enough to produce, and then remove, a seven-point “protective” effect. Chapter 4 flagged this hazard for the sta cohort, where any comparison built around remaining on a statin for some minimum duration is vulnerable to the same mechanism, and left for this chapter the question of which row of the target trial table is violated. It is the Follow-up row, which specifies when person-time starts accruing toward the outcome. Immortal time bias arises whenever the Assignment row — how a patient gets classified into a treatment strategy — is allowed to depend on something observed after the Follow-up row’s start date, rather than at it. A short checklist captures the requirement for any design in this book, ns, sta, or a design of your own: Component Must be fixed as of the same date as… Eligibility the date all inclusion criteria are first met Assignment the date the patient’s treatment strategy is classified Start of follow-up the date person-time begins accruing toward the outcome When those three dates coincide, as they do in ns by construction, immortal time cannot arise, because no interval separates the point at which a patient becomes eligible from the start of follow-up in which later information could influence the treatment label. If they are allowed to drift apart, as in the persistent-user hypothetical above, the resulting comparison can produce a spurious association or conceal a real one, and no adjustment method in Part II will correct it. This is much of what specifying a target trial buys: making eligibility, assignment, and the start of follow-up coincide forecloses immortal time bias rather than leaving it to be corrected after the fact, an argument developed by Hernán and colleagues (2016, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology). 6.5 Exercises Using what R/setup.R tells you about sta — that it follows patients who did or did not initiate a statin, with time variables cv_time, death_time, and loss_fu_time measured from cohort entry — describe whether sta follows a new-user or a prevalent-user design, and state what its time zero is. Chapter 7 Outcome regression and standardization Part I built the vocabulary: potential outcomes and estimands in Chapter 3, the target trial in Chapter 4, a diagram and an adjustment set in Chapter 5, and a design that earns the right to compare two arms in Chapter 6. What Part I did not do was produce an estimate, and that is the work of Part II. Over the next three chapters we answer the question we have been circling since Chapter 1 — does initiating a Cox-2 selective inhibitor, rather than a nonselective NSAID, change the risk of peptic ulcer disease? — three separate times, with three estimators that make the same identification assumptions and reach the same estimand by different routes: standardization here, propensity scores in Chapter 8, and inverse probability of treatment weighting in Chapter 9. The three are not competing philosophies. Each uses the covariates in ns_covs to address the imbalance documented in Chapter 6’s Table 1, and one reason to run all three is to see how little the answer moves when the estimator changes. We also start building the toolkit promised in the preface, with the book’s first estimator function, standardize(). 7.1 Adjusting with regression Let us start where most epidemiologic analyses start, with a regression model for the outcome. Chapter 6’s Table 1 told us that Cox-2 initiators are older, sicker, and more likely to be on corticosteroids than nonselective initiators, so the crude comparison of PUD risk between arms is confounded — and confounded in a direction we can anticipate, since patients were directed toward the Cox-2 drug partly because their physicians judged them to be at higher GI risk. ns |> group_by(cox2_init) |> summarise(n = n(), cases = sum(pud), risk = mean(pud), .groups = "drop") |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) cox2_init n cases risk 0 2642 258 0.098 1 240 30 0.125 The crude risks run 12.5% in the Cox-2 arm against 9.8% among nonselective initiators — a crude risk difference of +2.7 percentage points and a crude risk ratio of 1.28. Taken at face value, this suggests that the Cox-2 drug raises ulcer risk, which runs against its clinical rationale. It is a familiar pattern of confounding by indication, and it is the crude association that adjustment has to work on. The standard first step is a logistic model for pud that includes the treatment indicator alongside every covariate in the adjustment set. Rather than typing nineteen covariate names, we let reformulate() assemble the formula from ns_covs, which keeps R/setup.R as the single source of truth for what “adjusted” means in this book. library(broom) fit <- glm( reformulate(c("cox2_init", ns_covs), "pud"), family = binomial(), data = ns ) tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term %in% c("cox2_init", "age", "arthritisYes", "corticosteroid_useYes")) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high cox2_init 0.929 0.223 -0.331 0.74 0.591 1.418 age 1.066 0.005 13.321 0.00 1.056 1.076 arthritisYes 2.175 0.137 5.655 0.00 1.662 2.849 corticosteroid_useYes 3.202 0.620 1.879 0.06 0.837 10.036 Adjustment moves the estimate as expected. The coefficient on cox2_init, exponentiated, is an odds ratio of 0.93 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.42) — moved from the crude odds ratio of 1.32 to just below the null, though with an interval far too wide to rule out either a modest benefit or a modest harm. Age carries an odds ratio of 1.07 per year, and accounts for much of the confounding. There is a complication, however. That 0.93 is a conditional odds ratio: the odds ratio comparing two patients who are identical on all nineteen covariates and differ only in which NSAID they started. It is not the marginal contrast we defined in Chapter 3. The ATE was written \(E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]\), an average over the whole population of what would happen under each treatment, and therefore a quantity attached to a population rather than to a stratum. No coefficient in the regression provides it, and the discrepancy is not merely a matter of rescaling from odds to risks. The reason is noncollapsibility. If treatment truly has no effect, the conditional and marginal odds ratios agree at 1. Otherwise, even with no confounding at all, the odds ratio averaged over strata is pulled toward the null relative to the odds ratio within any stratum, simply because the odds scale is nonlinear and the strata have different baseline risks. The conditional odds ratio and the marginal odds ratio are answering different questions, and the difference between them does not indicate bias in either; it is a property of the scale. Greenland, Robins, and Pearl (1999) are the standard reference for keeping this distinction straight, and for the point that noncollapsibility and confounding are different phenomena that the same numerical gap can express. Risk differences and risk ratios do not behave this way; they collapse. Since the difficulty lies in reading the estimand off a coefficient rather than in the model itself, we can keep the fitted model and extract the marginal contrast from it directly, which is what standardization does. 7.2 Standardization: predict, then average The recipe, in words, is four steps. Fit an outcome model that includes treatment and the covariates. Then take the entire cohort and set every patient’s treatment to 1 — including the patients who actually took the nonselective drug — and ask the model to predict each patient’s risk in that hypothetical world. Take the whole cohort again, set everyone’s treatment to 0, and predict again. Average each set of predictions and contrast the two averages. This is the parametric g-formula, due to Robins (1986): the model is used only as a device for interpolating what each individual’s risk would have been under each treatment, and the averaging — over the observed covariate distribution of the whole cohort — is what turns those individual predictions into a marginal, population-level contrast. In code it takes five lines. ns1 <- ns |> mutate(cox2_init = 1) ns0 <- ns |> mutate(cox2_init = 0) risk1 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata = ns1, type = "response")) risk0 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata = ns0, type = "response")) c(risk0 = risk0, risk1 = risk1, rd = risk1 - risk0, rr = risk1 / risk0) ## risk0 risk1 rd rr ## 0.100531704 0.095016560 -0.005515145 0.945140244 Notice what the two copies of the data are doing. ns1 is the cohort as it would look if every one of these 2882 patients had started a Cox-2 inhibitor, with every covariate left exactly as observed; ns0 is the same cohort under the nonselective strategy. Because both averages are taken over the same covariate distribution — every patient, once, in each world — the difference between them cannot be attributed to a difference in case mix. This is the same logic as classical direct standardization to a reference population, with the fitted model standing in for the stratum-specific rates. Every step of that reasoning rests on Chapter 3’s identification conditions. Consistency lets us read a predicted risk under cox2_init = 1 as a potential outcome; conditional exchangeability, which Chapter 5’s diagram is our argument for, is what makes a model fit partly to treated patients usable for predicting untreated ones. Positivity bears on whether the resulting predictions can be trusted: with only 240 Cox-2 initiators among 2882 patients, the model extrapolates substantially when it predicts a Cox-2 world for covariate patterns in which almost no Cox-2 initiator was observed. Standardization will return an estimate regardless, which is a reason to keep Chapter 6’s Table 1 in view rather than relying on the estimator alone. We are going to want this in Chapters 8 and 9, so let us package it. The function takes the data, a model formula, and the name of the treatment column, and returns one row per estimand. Two details are worth pausing on. The "{treat}" := 1 syntax inside mutate() is dplyr’s glue notation for assigning to a column whose name is held in a variable, which is what lets the same function work for cox2_init here and statin later. And the point estimates are wrapped in their own inner function, point_estimates(), because the bootstrap in the next section needs to run exactly the same computation on a resampled data set — fitting the model inside the resample, not reusing the original fit. standardize <- function(data, outcome_model, treat, family = binomial(), n_boot = 200, conf_level = 0.95, seed = NULL) { if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed) point_estimates <- function(d) { fit <- glm(outcome_model, family = family, data = d) d1 <- d |> mutate("{treat}" := 1) d0 <- d |> mutate("{treat}" := 0) risk1 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata = d1, type = "response")) risk0 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata = d0, type = "response")) c(risk0 = risk0, risk1 = risk1, rd = risk1 - risk0, rr = risk1 / risk0) } est <- point_estimates(data) boot_est <- replicate(n_boot, { point_estimates(slice_sample(data, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)) }) alpha <- 1 - conf_level tibble( estimand = names(est), estimate = unname(est), conf_low = apply(boot_est, 1, quantile, probs = alpha / 2), conf_high = apply(boot_est, 1, quantile, probs = 1 - alpha / 2) ) } That code lives in R/standardize.R, so from here on we source it rather than retype it. source("R/standardize.R") std <- standardize( ns, outcome_model = reformulate(c("cox2_init", ns_covs), "pud"), treat = "cox2_init", n_boot = 200, seed = 921 ) std |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) estimand estimate conf_low conf_high risk0 0.101 0.090 0.112 risk1 0.095 0.064 0.124 rd -0.006 -0.038 0.025 rr 0.945 0.624 1.240 Here is the estimate, on the scale Chapter 3 called for. Had every patient in ns started a nonselective NSAID, the model puts PUD risk at 10.1%; had every one of them started a Cox-2 inhibitor, 9.5%. The standardized risk difference is -0.6 percentage points (95% CI -3.8 to +2.5) and the standardized risk ratio 0.95 (0.62 to 1.24). Adjustment has moved the crude risk ratio of 1.28 to 0.95 — from apparent harm to a point estimate slightly on the protective side of the null — but the interval comfortably includes 1, so these data support no more than the absence of a large effect in either direction, and certainly not a benefit. With 288 ulcer cases and 240 Cox-2 initiators, this is close to the precision the cohort can provide. Note also what noncollapsibility looks like in the arithmetic. The standardized risks imply a marginal odds ratio of 0.939, while the regression coefficient gave a conditional odds ratio of 0.929, the conditional one sitting slightly further from the null, as expected. The gap is small here only because PUD is uncommon; with a common outcome it can be substantial. 7.3 The bootstrap The point estimates came out of a glm() fit, so it is tempting to reach for that model’s standard errors, but they do not apply here. The standardized risk difference is not a parameter of the logistic model at all — it is a nonlinear function of every coefficient in the model, combined with the empirical covariate distribution of the cohort. There is no line in the summary() output whose standard error describes it, and the delta-method calculation that would produce one by hand is tedious and specification-specific. Resampling avoids the algebra. The sampling variability of our estimate arises because ns is one draw of 2882 patients from some larger population, so we mimic that draw by sampling 2882 patients from ns with replacement, and recompute the whole estimator — refit the model, re-predict both worlds, re-average, re-contrast — on each resample. The spread of those recomputed estimates approximates the spread we would see across repeated samples from the population, and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of that spread give a 95% percentile confidence interval. It is important that everything downstream of sampling be redone within each replicate, model fitting included; bootstrapping only the averaging step, with the coefficients held fixed, would ignore the largest source of uncertainty in the procedure. n_boot trades precision for time. Each replicate is a full glm() fit on 2882 rows, and our default of 200 is enough to place an interval roughly while keeping a book that re-renders often tolerable to build. The percentile endpoints are themselves noisy at that size, though, so a different seed will shift them in the second decimal place; for a result you intend to publish, 1,000 or 2,000 is the right order of magnitude, and seed is what makes whichever number you choose reproducible. 7.4 Effect modification So far we have estimated one effect for everybody. But the effect of a Cox-2 inhibitor might plausibly differ by whether a patient is also taking aspirin, since aspirin damages gastric mucosa through the same prostaglandin pathway the Cox-2 drug was designed to spare. When a causal effect differs across levels of a covariate, we call that effect modification (or heterogeneity of treatment effect), and we look for it by letting the treatment coefficient depend on that covariate — an interaction term. fit_int <- glm( reformulate(c("cox2_init", ns_covs, "cox2_init:aspirin_use"), "pud"), family = binomial(), data = ns ) tidy(fit_int, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(str_detect(term, "cox2_init")) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high cox2_init 0.936 0.228 -0.291 0.771 0.588 1.443 cox2_init:aspirin_useYes 0.870 0.995 -0.140 0.889 0.098 5.480 The interaction term is a ratio of odds ratios, 0.87 with a p-value of 0.89 — no evidence of modification, which is unsurprising given that only 92 of the 2882 patients use aspirin and only 9 of those started a Cox-2 inhibitor. The coefficient is in any case not the quantity of interest, for the reason given above: it is a conditional, noncollapsible quantity on the odds scale. The subgroup effects of interest are two standardized risk differences, one within each aspirin stratum. Standardizing within a subgroup means changing the population we average over: instead of predicting both worlds for the whole cohort, we predict both worlds for the aspirin users only, then repeat for the non-users. Fitting a separate model within each stratum is the fully flexible version of the interaction above — it lets every coefficient, not just treatment’s, differ by aspirin use — so we can get subgroup effects by calling standardize() on each subset. One adjustment is forced on us: aspirin_use is constant within a stratum by construction and has to leave the covariate list, and among aspirin users anti_coagulant_use turns out to be constant too. With only 92 aspirin users we cannot support nineteen covariates in that stratum in any case. We fit a deliberately lean model in both strata so the two are comparable. lean <- reformulate(c("cox2_init", "age", "sex", "arthritis"), "pud") sub <- bind_rows( standardize(filter(ns, aspirin_use == "No"), lean, "cox2_init", seed = 922) |> mutate(aspirin = "No", .before = 1), standardize(filter(ns, aspirin_use == "Yes"), lean, "cox2_init", seed = 923) |> mutate(aspirin = "Yes", .before = 1) ) sub |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) aspirin estimand estimate conf_low conf_high No risk0 0.098 0.087 0.108 No risk1 0.091 0.061 0.120 No rd -0.007 -0.040 0.021 No rr 0.930 0.609 1.214 Yes risk0 0.196 0.117 0.276 Yes risk1 0.193 0.000 0.353 Yes rd -0.003 -0.204 0.165 Yes rr 0.986 0.000 2.048 Aspirin users start from a much higher baseline: a standardized nonselective-NSAID risk of 19.6% against 9.8% among non-users, which is consistent with the pathway described above. The standardized risk differences, though, are -0.3 points among aspirin users and -0.7 points among non-users, and the aspirin-user interval runs from -20.4 to +16.5 percentage points — wide enough to contain nearly any clinically meaningful effect in either direction. The risk ratio row is worse still, with a lower bound at essentially zero: in some resamples the handful of aspirin-using Cox-2 initiators produced a predicted risk near zero, and the bootstrap reports that instability faithfully. The wide interval reflects the sparsity of the data rather than anything about the drug. We suppressed R’s separation warnings in that chunk to keep the output readable, although they convey the same information. It is worth being precise about how effect modification differs from confounding, because both get described loosely as “a covariate that matters.” Confounding is a problem of identification: a common cause of treatment and outcome makes the observed contrast fail to equal the causal one, and we adjust for it to recover a valid estimate. Effect modification, in contrast, is not a threat to validity; it is a feature of the causal effect itself. A confounder must be addressed or the estimate will be biased, whereas an effect modifier is something we choose to report, and the estimand changes when we do, from one ATE for the cohort to a set of subgroup-specific ATEs. A variable can be one, the other, or both: aspirin use here is a candidate for either role. Note also that the overall standardized risk difference of -0.6 points is a weighted average of the subgroup effects, weighted by how common each subgroup is — which is why a cohort-level ATE can be small while an effect in a small subgroup is large, and why the population one standardizes to is part of the estimand rather than an implementation choice. 7.5 Exercises The model above enters age linearly on the log-odds scale. Refit it with poly(age, 2) in place of age and rerun standardize() with the same seed. How much do the standardized risks and the risk difference move? Does the confidence interval change enough to alter what you would conclude, and what does your answer suggest about how sensitive this estimate is to the functional form of the strongest confounder? ppi_use and h2_antagonist_use are gastroprotective drugs, so they may be markers of a physician’s concern about GI risk rather than causes of it. Drop both from the covariate list and rerun standardize(). Report the standardized risk difference with and without them. This is an informal sensitivity analysis to the choice of adjustment set; using Chapter 5’s language, sketch the DAG under which including them is right and the DAG under which it is wrong. Modify point_estimates() inside a copy of standardize() so that the two predicted risks are averaged over filter(d, cox2_init == 1) while the model is still fit on all of d, and estimate the ATT for the Cox-2 question. Chapter 8 Propensity scores Chapter 7 adjusted for confounding by modeling the outcome. We wrote down a logistic regression for pud that included the treatment indicator and all nineteen covariates in ns_covs, then averaged its predictions over the cohort twice. It worked, but notice how much weight that single model was carrying: nineteen covariates and their functional forms, all of it resting on 288 ulcer cases. This chapter takes a second route to the same question, and it moves the modeling burden to the other side of the problem. Instead of modeling how covariates produce the outcome, we model how covariates produce treatment, and then use that one fitted probability — rather than the nineteen covariates themselves — to make the arms comparable. In many studies the appeal is arithmetic, because exposure is far more common than the outcome and the treatment model therefore has more information to work with; here, with 240 Cox-2 initiators against 288 cases, the two are comparably rare and the appeal is conceptual instead. The gain is a separation between the work of making the groups comparable and the work of estimating an effect. 8.1 One number that summarizes confounding The propensity score is the probability of receiving treatment given the measured covariates, \[e(L) = P(A = 1 \mid L),\] a single number between 0 and 1 attached to each patient. In our cohort it is the probability that a patient with this age, sex, region, comorbidity profile, and medication history was started on a Cox-2 selective inhibitor rather than a nonselective NSAID. What makes this useful is a result of Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983): the propensity score is a balancing score. Among patients who share the same value of \(e(L)\), the distribution of \(L\) itself is the same in the treated and the untreated. Two patients with a propensity score of 0.20 may look nothing alike — one old with arthritis and no other illness, the other younger with diabetes and hypertension — but if we collect everyone whose score is 0.20, the treated members of that collection and the untreated members will have, on average, the same age distribution, the same arthritis prevalence, the same steroid use, and so on for every covariate that went into the score. Within a level of the score, treatment is as though randomized with respect to those covariates. The consequence for us is the second half of the theorem. If conditional exchangeability holds given the full covariate vector \(L\) — Chapter 3’s assumption, for which Chapter 5’s diagram is the argument — then it also holds given \(e(L)\) alone. So we may condition on a single scalar in place of nineteen variables without loss, reducing nineteen dimensions of confounding to one number. Two cautions belong here at the outset. First, the propensity score is a nuisance parameter: a patient’s probability of receiving a Cox-2 inhibitor is of no interest in itself, and the coefficients of the treatment model should not be interpreted causally, since the score serves only as something to condition on. Second, the balancing property holds for the true score, which we do not observe. We estimate it, and the justification for the estimate rests less on the model being correctly specified than on its demonstrably balancing the covariates, which is something we can check directly and do check below. 8.2 Estimating the score Estimating a propensity score is a logistic regression like any other, so the function that does it is short. It fits the treatment model and returns the data with the fitted probabilities attached as a column named ps, which is what every method later in the chapter consumes. est_ps <- function(data, treat_model) { fit <- glm(treat_model, family = binomial(), data = data) data |> mutate(ps = predict(fit, type = "response")) } predict() with type = "response" is what puts the predictions on the probability scale rather than the log-odds scale; without it we would get linear predictors, which balance just as well but are harder to read. That code and the matching function below live in R/propensity.R, so from here on we source it. source("R/propensity.R") ps_model <- reformulate(ns_covs, "cox2_init") ns_ps <- est_ps(ns, ps_model) |> mutate(id = row_number()) ns_ps |> group_by(cox2_init) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_ps = mean(ps), min = min(ps), max = max(ps), .groups = "drop") |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) cox2_init n mean_ps min max 0 2642 0.081 0.016 0.423 1 240 0.109 0.029 0.506 Notice the formula. reformulate(ns_covs, "cox2_init") puts treatment on the left and the covariates on the right, the mirror image of Chapter 7’s outcome model and with no mention of pud anywhere. This is more than a technicality, because the model can be built, inspected, and revised without ever looking at the outcome, so it cannot be tuned, however unconsciously, toward an answer we like. Propensity-score analysis therefore restores something outcome modeling gives up: a design stage, prior to and separate from analysis, in which we work only with treatment and covariates, and which is as close as an observational study comes to specifying a randomization scheme. Rubin (2008) makes this the central argument for propensity scores — that in observational work design trumps analysis, and that the discipline of settling the comparison before the outcome is ever examined is most of what the score is for. The fitted scores average 0.109 in the Cox-2 arm against 0.081 among nonselective initiators, straddling the cohort-wide treatment prevalence of 8.3%. That separation is the confounding of Chapter 6’s Table 1, now expressed as one number: the model can distinguish the arms because the arms genuinely differ. Of more interest is how much the two distributions overlap. ggplot(ns_ps, aes(x = ps, fill = factor(cox2_init))) + geom_density(alpha = 0.45, colour = NA) + scale_fill_discrete(name = NULL, labels = c("Nonselective NSAID", "Cox-2 selective")) + labs(x = "Estimated propensity score", y = "Density") + theme_minimal() This plot is where the positivity assumption becomes visible, and it is the first thing to examine before any propensity-score analysis: the region of the score occupied by treated patients should also be occupied by untreated patients, and conversely, since conditioning on the score is informative only where both arms are represented. Formally the ranges nest: the count of nonselective initiators above the highest treated score is 0, and the count of Cox-2 initiators below the lowest untreated score is 0. The tails, however, are where the assumption becomes thin. The bottom percentile of the score holds 29 patients, of whom 0 started a Cox-2 inhibitor; the top percentile holds 29 patients, of whom 5 did. The left tail therefore contains patients for whom we have almost no information about what a Cox-2 inhibitor would have done, and the right tail is sparse in the other direction. Chapter 7’s standardization encountered the same problem, but silently, extrapolating wherever it had to. Here the difficulty can be seen on a plot, which is one reason to estimate a propensity score even when one intends to adjust in some other way. 8.3 Stratification The most direct use of a balancing score is to stratify on it. If treated and untreated patients within a level of the score are comparable, then a risk difference computed inside a narrow band of the score is unconfounded, and we can pool those within-band differences into one estimate. Bands of exactly equal score would be empty, so in practice we cut the score into quantiles — quintiles, conventionally. strata <- ns_ps |> mutate(ps_q = ntile(ps, 5)) |> group_by(ps_q) |> summarise( n_treat = sum(cox2_init), n_ctrl = sum(1 - cox2_init), risk1 = mean(pud[cox2_init == 1]), risk0 = mean(pud[cox2_init == 0]), rd = risk1 - risk0, var_rd = risk1 * (1 - risk1) / n_treat + risk0 * (1 - risk0) / n_ctrl, .groups = "drop" ) strata |> select(-var_rd) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) ps_q n_treat n_ctrl risk1 risk0 rd 1 13 564 0.077 0.035 0.041 2 29 548 0.034 0.058 -0.024 3 36 540 0.028 0.078 -0.050 4 77 499 0.130 0.106 0.024 5 85 491 0.200 0.226 -0.026 Read down the risk0 column first. Baseline risk climbs steadily from 3.5% in the lowest-propensity quintile to 22.6% in the highest, which is the confounding made concrete: the covariates that pushed physicians toward the Cox-2 drug are the same covariates that predict ulcers. Read the n_treat column next and the cost of stratification becomes clear. The lowest quintile holds only 13 Cox-2 initiators against 564 nonselective ones, so its risk difference of +4.1 percentage points rests on a handful of patients and should not be interpreted on its own. Pooling is therefore necessary, and the choice of how to pool determines the estimand. Weighting each stratum by the inverse of its variance — precision weighting, the logic behind the Mantel–Haenszel estimator — gives the most statistically efficient combination: c(rd_precision_weighted = rd_prec, se = se_prec) ## rd_precision_weighted se ## -0.02074445 0.01777657 That is -2.1 percentage points with a standard error of 1.8, so a 95% interval running roughly -5.6 to +1.4 points. Weighting each stratum by its size instead gives -0.7 points, considerably closer to Chapter 7’s standardized risk difference of -0.6. Neither is wrong, but they answer different questions. The size-weighted average is standardization to the cohort’s own covariate distribution, and so estimates the ATE of Chapter 3. The precision-weighted average is standardized to a population defined by where the information happens to be, which coincides with the ATE only if the risk difference is constant across strata. When effects vary across strata, efficiency and interpretability diverge, and it is worth stating which of the two has been chosen. Either way, both sit on the protective side of the null while the crude risk difference was +2.7 points, and both have intervals wide enough to include no effect. Whether the stratification balances the covariates can be checked directly. Because the score is a balancing score, covariates should be similar between arms within a stratum even though they differ sharply overall. We apply Chapter 2’s table1_categorical() to the top quintile. source("R/table1.R") top_q <- ns_ps |> mutate(ps_q = ntile(ps, 5)) |> filter(ps_q == 5) table1_categorical(top_q, c("arthritis", "corticosteroid_use", "hypertension"), by = "cox2_init") |> knitr::kable() variable level 0 1 arthritis No 109 (22.2%) 24 (28.2%) arthritis Yes 382 (77.8%) 61 (71.8%) corticosteroid_use No 478 (97.4%) 80 (94.1%) corticosteroid_use Yes 13 (2.6%) 5 (5.9%) hypertension No 289 (58.9%) 56 (65.9%) hypertension Yes 202 (41.1%) 29 (34.1%) table1_continuous(top_q, "age", by = "cox2_init") |> knitr::kable() variable 0 1 age 63.2 (13.5) 62.1 (13.7) The balance is much improved. Across the whole cohort, Cox-2 initiators are 6.1 years older on average and 17 percentage points more likely to carry an arthritis diagnosis. Within the top propensity quintile the age gap has shrunk to 1.1 years, and in the opposite direction, while the arthritis, steroid, and hypertension percentages are within a few points of each other. Both arms of this stratum consist of high-propensity patients and are therefore older and more often arthritic, so much of what distinguished the arms overall has been absorbed into the stratum itself. Balance within quintiles is good but necessarily imperfect. Patients with scores of 0.12 and 0.50 fall in the same top quintile despite differing considerably, so some confounding remains within each band; Cochran’s (1968) classic result is that five strata remove roughly 90% of the bias from a single continuous confounder, leaving the remainder. Matching addresses that residual by making comparisons between individuals rather than within bands. 8.4 Matching Matching pairs each treated patient with an untreated patient whose propensity score is close, and analyzes the paired sample. The version below is the simplest form that remains defensible: greedy 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching without replacement, within a caliper. # Greedy 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching without replacement. ps_match <- function(data, treat, ps = "ps", caliper = 0.05) { treated <- data |> filter(.data[[treat]] == 1) |> arrange(desc(.data[[ps]])) controls <- data |> filter(.data[[treat]] == 0) used <- rep(FALSE, nrow(controls)) pairs <- vector("list", nrow(treated)) for (i in seq_len(nrow(treated))) { dist <- abs(controls[[ps]] - treated[[ps]][i]) dist[used] <- Inf j <- which.min(dist) if (dist[j] <= caliper) { used[j] <- TRUE pairs[[i]] <- bind_rows(treated[i, ], controls[j, ]) } } bind_rows(pairs, .id = "pair_id") } Four decisions are encoded in those lines. Greedy means we take treated patients one at a time and give each its closest available control, never revisiting an earlier choice; it is not guaranteed to minimize total distance the way optimal matching would, but it is transparent and fast. Without replacement is enforced by the used vector, which sets already-matched controls to infinite distance so no control appears twice — keeping the paired analysis honest at the cost of using fewer controls. The arrange(desc()) orders treated patients from the highest score down, so the hardest patients to match, the ones out at the sparse end of the distribution, get first pick of the control pool. The caliper sets a limit on how poor a match will be accepted: if the nearest available control differs by more than 0.05 on the propensity scale, that treated patient is left unmatched rather than paired with an implausible comparator. Unmatched patients are how a matched analysis registers a positivity problem rather than extrapolating past one. matched <- ps_match(ns_ps, treat = "cox2_init", caliper = 0.05) n_pairs <- n_distinct(matched$pair_id) c(pairs = n_pairs, treated_available = sum(ns_ps$cox2_init), unmatched = sum(ns_ps$cox2_init) - n_pairs) ## pairs treated_available unmatched ## 239 240 1 The matching yields 239 pairs from 240 Cox-2 initiators, a shortfall of 1: at the extreme right of the density plot there is a treated patient for whom no nonselective initiator falls inside the caliper. With balance established, the effect estimate is a comparison of two proportions in the matched sample. matched |> group_by(cox2_init) |> summarise(n = n(), cases = sum(pud), risk = mean(pud), .groups = "drop") |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) cox2_init n cases risk 0 239 40 0.167 1 239 30 0.126 The matched risk difference is -4.2 percentage points, 12.6% against 16.7%, with a risk ratio of 0.75. Because the sample is paired, the standard error should respect the pairing: we take the within-pair difference in outcomes for each of the 239 pairs and compute the standard error of their mean, 3.1 percentage points, giving an interval of roughly -10.3 to +1.9 points. It comfortably includes zero. That point estimate is further from the null than the -0.6 points standardization gave us, and two things account for the gap. The first is precision: we discarded 2404 patients, so the matched interval is much wider than Chapter 7’s and the point estimate correspondingly less stable. The second is that matching estimates a different estimand. Every treated patient is kept and controls are recruited to resemble them, so the covariate distribution we have averaged over is that of the Cox-2 initiators — the ATT of Chapter 3, not the ATE. Given that the Cox-2 arm is older and sicker, and therefore at higher baseline risk, there is no reason to expect the ATT and the ATE to agree, and the matched estimate should not be read as a failed replication of the standardized one. It answers a related question, and in many settings the more clinically relevant one: what the drug did for the patients who actually received it. 8.5 Choosing the PS model Everything above depends on which variables enter ps_model, and the selection rule is not to include whatever predicts treatment best. Judging a propensity-score model by its c-statistic is misleading, because a model that separated the arms perfectly would push the two densities apart until they no longer overlapped, removing the comparability the method depends on. A propensity-score model is adequate if it produces balance and preserves overlap, which is what the love plot and the density plot were used to assess. Chapter 5’s diagram guides what belongs in the model. Confounders — common causes of treatment and outcome, such as age, arthritis, and steroid use — must be included. Pure outcome predictors, variables that affect the outcome but not treatment, should generally be included as well, since they cannot introduce bias and conditioning on them improves precision. The variables to leave out are instruments: variables that influence treatment but have no effect on the outcome except through treatment, of which physician prescribing preference is the standard example. Including an instrument improves the fit of the treatment model, and that is why it causes trouble: it spreads the propensity scores apart, reduces overlap, inflates the variance of the estimate, and can amplify bias from unmeasured confounding. As in Chapter 5, colliders and variables on the causal pathway from treatment to outcome are excluded; the propensity score provides no exemption from the rules for reading a DAG. That last consequence has a name of its own. Bias amplification refers to more than a loss of precision: conditioning on an instrument-like variable can make the bias from an unmeasured confounder larger than it was before adjustment. The instrument accounts for the part of the variation in treatment that was unrelated to the confounder, so the residual variation is more heavily loaded with the unmeasured confounder, and the estimate then contrasts patients who differ more on \(U\) than the full cohort did. Brookhart et al. (2006, AJE) demonstrated the effect in simulation, which is why advice to include everything that predicts treatment can do real damage rather than merely waste degrees of freedom. The opposite extreme is also defensible in the right setting: in large claims databases, high-dimensional proxy adjustment — the hd-PS algorithm of Schneeweiss et al. (2009) — screens thousands of diagnosis and dispensing codes for empirical proxies of unmeasured confounders and selects a few hundred, on the argument that no investigator can enumerate them by hand. That approach is beyond this book’s scope, but it is where the course’s variable-selection session lands, and the tension between it and the diagram-first rule above is a real one rather than a misunderstanding. Two habits follow. First, choose the covariate set from substantive knowledge and the diagram before looking at the outcome, which is what the design stage makes possible. Second, when a variable’s role is genuinely unclear, include it if it plausibly affects the outcome and exclude it if it plausibly affects only treatment, and report the analysis both ways. ns_covs was assembled on that reasoning, and its arguable members, among them ppi_use and h2_antagonist_use from Chapter 7’s exercises, are the ones worth varying. 8.6 Exercises Re-estimate the propensity score with arthritis removed from the covariate list, rematch, and compare the two love plots. How many treated patients are lost relative to the 0.05 caliper? Report each with an interval. State which estimand each one targets and rank them by precision, then say which you would report as the primary analysis and why. Suppose you are building a propensity-score model for the effect of a new osteoporosis treatment on fracture risk in a claims database covering ten years. Available at baseline are age, sex, prior fracture, bone density testing in the previous year, glucocorticoid use, falls recorded in the previous year, body mass index, calendar year of initiation, the prescribing physician’s volume of osteoporosis prescriptions, and a diagnosis of dementia recorded after the initiation date. For each variable, say whether it belongs in the treatment model, giving the role you are assigning it — confounder, pure predictor of the outcome, pure predictor of treatment, collider, or post-treatment variable. Then answer two questions in more detail. Prescribing patterns for this drug class changed substantially over the ten years: what does including calendar year buy, and what would omitting it cost? And physician prescribing volume predicts treatment strongly while having no plausible direct effect on fracture: what does including such a variable risk, in the terms of the bias-amplification discussion above, and under what conditions would you nonetheless include it?

Chapter 9 Inverse probability of treatment weighting Chapter 8 built a propensity score and used it in two ways, each of which discarded information: stratification coarsened the score into five bands, and matching dropped every nonselective initiator who failed to pair with a Cox-2 patient. This chapter puts the same fitted score to a third use that retains every patient. Although the earlier estimators worked by grouping people who resemble each other, here we leave the cohort intact and assign each patient a weight, larger for those who received the treatment their covariates made unlikely and smaller for those who received the expected one. In the reweighted cohort treatment and covariates are unrelated by construction, so a comparison of two weighted means estimates the causal contrast. This is inverse probability of treatment weighting, the last of Part II’s three estimators and the one that generalizes most readily, since it extends cleanly to treatments that change over time. 9.1 Reweighting to a pseudo-population The intuition is easiest to see in a cohort small enough to work by hand. Suppose the only confounder is frailty, present in 400 of 1,000 patients. Frail patients are treated with probability 0.60 and non-frail patients with probability 0.15, and the true risk of the outcome is 20% in frail patients and 10% in non-frail patients regardless of treatment — so the treatment does nothing at all. toy <- tibble( frail = c( 1, 1, 0, 0), arm = c( 1, 0, 1, 0), n = c(240, 160, 90, 510), cases = c( 48, 32, 9, 51) ) |> mutate( e = if_else(frail == 1, 0.60, 0.15), wt = if_else(arm == 1, 1 / e, 1 / (1 - e)), pseudo_n = n * wt, pseudo_y = cases * wt ) toy |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) frail arm n cases e wt pseudo_n pseudo_y 1 1 240 48 0.60 1.667 400 80 1 0 160 32 0.60 2.500 400 80 0 1 90 9 0.15 6.667 600 60 0 0 510 51 0.15 1.176 600 60 Compared crudely, treatment looks harmful: risk 17.3% among the treated against 12.4% among the untreated, a risk difference of +4.9 percentage points for a drug with no effect. The reason is entirely in the n column: the treated arm is nearly three-quarters frail, the untreated arm three-quarters not. Now read the wt column. A frail treated patient had probability 0.60 of ending up where she did, so she stands in for \(1/0.60 = 1.67\) patients like her; a frail untreated patient had probability 0.40, so she stands in for two and a half. Look at pseudo_n: both arms now contain 400 frail and 600 non-frail patients, 1,000 apiece — each arm inflated into a copy of the whole cohort. In this pseudo-population — Hernán and Robins’s term for the reweighted cohort — frailty is distributed identically across arms; the association between frailty and treatment has been broken by duplicating patients rather than by conditioning on frailty, and the weighted risks come out at 14.0% and 14.0%, a risk difference of exactly zero. That is the essential idea, and the general form of the weight follows directly. For a patient with covariates \(L\) who received treatment \(A\) the weight is \[W = \frac{1}{P(A \mid L)} = \frac{A}{e(L)} + \frac{1-A}{1 - e(L)},\] the reciprocal of the probability of the treatment actually received, which is where the estimator’s name comes from. Each patient represents herself plus everyone with her covariates who would have gone the other way, and Chapter 3’s identification conditions license that substitution: consistency, conditional exchangeability given \(L\), and positivity. Positivity is doing conspicuous work here, because as \(e(L)\) approaches zero for a treated patient her weight grows without bound, and a handful of patients can come to speak for the entire pseudo-population. 9.2 Building the weights The weight above, \(1/P(A \mid L)\), is the unstabilized weight. It averages to about 2, because each arm is inflated to the size of the full cohort and the pseudo-population is therefore roughly twice the real one. Nothing is wrong with that, although it makes the weights larger and more variable than they need to be, and variability in the weights inflates the variance of the estimate. Stabilized weights fix this by multiplying by the marginal probability of the treatment received, \[W^{s} = \frac{P(A)}{P(A \mid L)} = A\,\frac{\Pr(A=1)}{e(L)} + (1-A)\,\frac{1 - \Pr(A=1)}{1 - e(L)}.\] The numerator does not depend on covariates, so it cannot undo the balancing the denominator achieves; it does no more than rescale each arm so that the pseudo-population is about the size of the real cohort. The diagnostic consequence is convenient: stabilized weights should average close to 1, and a mean far from 1 is a sign that the treatment model is misbehaving. Cole and Hernán (2008) are the practical reference for constructing these weights and for reading their mean this way. Our estimator packages the whole procedure — fit the treatment model, form the weights, optionally truncate them, and fit a weighted regression of the outcome on treatment alone. iptw_estimator <- function(data, treat_model, outcome, treat, family = gaussian(), stabilize = TRUE, truncate_at = NULL) { data <- est_ps(data, treat_model) p_treat <- mean(data[[treat]]) data <- data |> mutate( wt = if_else(.data[[treat]] == 1, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps)), wt = if (stabilize) { if_else(.data[[treat]] == 1, p_treat * wt, (1 - p_treat) * wt) } else wt ) if (!is.null(truncate_at)) { data <- data |> mutate(wt = pmin(wt, quantile(wt, truncate_at))) } fit <- geepack::geeglm( reformulate(treat, outcome), id = seq_len(nrow(data)), weights = data$wt, family = family, data = data ) broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE) } Three details deserve comment. The function calls Chapter 8’s est_ps() rather than fitting its own logistic model, which keeps one definition of “propensity score” in the book. The outcome regression is reformulate(treat, outcome) — treatment and nothing else, because the weights have already dealt with the covariates; a weighted regression that also adjusted for ns_covs would be a different, doubly adjusted estimator. And the fit goes through geepack::geeglm() with id = seq_len(nrow(data)), making every patient her own cluster under an independent working correlation. That is an elaborate way to reproduce a glm() point estimate, but it delivers the sandwich standard error, which is what we need here. A weighted glm() treats the weights as counts of real observations and reports intervals that are far too narrow, whereas the robust variance from geeglm() is estimated empirically rather than from the weighted likelihood. That code lives in R/iptw_estimator.R. Before using it, we look at the weights themselves. source("R/propensity.R") ps_model <- reformulate(ns_covs, "cox2_init") wts <- est_ps(ns, ps_model) |> mutate( p_treat = mean(cox2_init), w_unstab = if_else(cox2_init == 1, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps)), w_stab = if_else(cox2_init == 1, p_treat * w_unstab, (1 - p_treat) * w_unstab) ) summary(wts$w_unstab) ## Min. 1st Qu. The maxima are more informative: 34.2 unstabilized against 2.8 stabilized. That largest unstabilized weight belongs to the Cox-2 initiator whose estimated propensity score is 0.029 — a patient whose covariates made the Cox-2 drug very unlikely, who received it anyway, and who is therefore asked to represent thirty-odd patients like herself who did not. Kish’s effective sample size, \((\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2\), falls from 2882 unweighted to 2823 under stabilized weights and all the way to 756 unstabilized: a compact measure of how much information a few large weights consume. The histogram shows where the asymmetry lies. The patient with the largest weight sits in the sparse left tail of Chapter 8’s density plot, where matching declined to find a partner. Matching reported that difficulty by leaving her out, whereas weighting reports it by making her highly influential, which is easier to miss, so the weight distribution should be printed and plotted routinely. 9.3 Estimating the effect With the weights in hand the effect estimate is a weighted regression of pud on cox2_init and nothing else. The link function chooses the scale: an identity link on a 0/1 outcome — family = gaussian() — gives the treatment coefficient as a risk difference, and a log link with poisson() gives it as a log risk ratio, which we exponentiate. source("R/propensity.R"); source("R/iptw_estimator.R") ps_model <- reformulate(ns_covs, "cox2_init") iptw_estimator(ns, ps_model, outcome = "pud", treat = "cox2_init", family = gaussian()) |> knitr::kable(digits = 4) term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high (Intercept) 0.1018 0.006 286.7239 0.0000 0.0900 0.1136 cox2_init -0.0029 0.020 0.0202 0.8869 -0.0421 0.0364 iptw_estimator(ns, ps_model, outcome = "pud", treat = "cox2_init", family = poisson(link = "log")) |> mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), exp)) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3) term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high (Intercept) 0.102 0.059 1496.629 0.000 0.091 0.114 cox2_init 0.972 0.202 0.020 0.888 0.654 1.444 The weighted risk difference is -0.29 percentage points, with a 95% interval from -4.2 to +3.6 points, and the weighted risk ratio is 0.97 (0.65 to 1.44). Both estimates sit essentially on the null. The Poisson fit deserves a note. The outcome is binary rather than a count, so the likelihood is deliberately wrong, although the coefficient of a log-link regression on a 0/1 outcome still estimates a log risk ratio, and the sandwich variance repairs the standard error that the wrong likelihood would give. This is the modified Poisson approach to risk ratios, and it is a further reason for the geeglm() machinery. There is very little on the outcome side of this analysis: the regression has one covariate. Everything we know about age, arthritis, steroids, and the other seventeen variables entered through the weights, which were built without ever looking at pud, so Chapter 8’s design-stage discipline carries through to the estimate. 9.4 Truncation and diagnostics The obvious response to a weight of 34.2 is to cap it. Truncation replaces every weight above a chosen percentile with the value at that percentile; our function does this with pmin(wt, quantile(wt, truncate_at)) when truncate_at is supplied. iptw_estimator(ns, ps_model, outcome = "pud", treat = "cox2_init", family = gaussian(), truncate_at = 0.99) |> knitr::kable(digits = 4) term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high (Intercept) 0.1018 0.0060 286.7243 0.0000 0.0900 0.1136 cox2_init -0.0002 0.0202 0.0002 0.9902 -0.0398 0.0393 Capping at the 99th percentile touches 29 of the 2882 patients and moves the risk difference from -0.29 to -0.02 percentage points, with the standard error changing from 0.0200 to 0.0202. Truncation therefore buys almost nothing in this cohort, which is itself informative: the estimate is robust to the handful of most influential patients. The trade-off deserves to be stated explicitly, since truncation is a deliberate exchange of bias for variance. If the treatment model is correct, the untruncated estimator is consistent for the ATE and the truncated one is not, because we have knowingly misrepresented how much of the pseudo-population the extreme patients should represent. What we get in return is stability, and when a single weight dominates the sum a small amount of bias can be worth accepting. Truncation is therefore better used as a sensitivity analysis than as a default: report the untruncated estimate, report it capped at the 99th and 95th percentiles, and if they disagree materially, say so. An estimate that depends on whether one patient counts thirty times or ten is being driven by extrapolation into a region where the data are thin, and no choice of cap will remedy that. Trimming, which drops patients outside a range of the propensity score altogether, is the other common option; it changes the population and therefore the estimand, and should be described as such. The distinction is worth holding onto, since the two words are not always kept apart: truncation caps a weight and keeps the patient, trimming discards the patient — often those outside a percentile range of the propensity score — and both the course and much of the literature use “trimming” loosely for either operation, so it is worth saying which one you did. 9.5 Standardized mortality ratio weights The weights built so far blow both arms up into a copy of the whole cohort, which is why they estimate the ATE. A small change to the weight redirects the estimator at a different population. Leave the treated arm alone — every treated patient keeps weight 1 — and give each untreated patient \(e(L) / (1 - e(L))\), the odds of treatment her covariates imply. The untreated are then reweighted to resemble the treated rather than the cohort, the treated covariate distribution becomes the standard, and the estimand is the ATT: the effect of treatment among the treated. In the course these are called SMR (standardized mortality ratio) weights, after the indirect standardization that gives a standardized mortality ratio its name. source("R/propensity.R") smr <- est_ps(ns, ps_model) |> mutate(w_smr = if_else(cox2_init == 1, 1, ps / (1 - ps))) smr_fit <- geepack::geeglm( pud ~ cox2_init, id = seq_len(nrow(smr)), weights = smr$w_smr, family = gaussian(), data = smr ) broom::tidy(smr_fit, conf.int = TRUE) |> knitr::kable(digits = 4) term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high (Intercept) 0.1473 0.0100 218.6235 0.0000 0.1277 0.1668 cox2_init -0.0223 0.0236 0.8924 0.3448 -0.0684 0.0239 The SMR-weighted risk difference is -2.23 percentage points (-6.8 to +2.4). Set beside the ATE of -0.29 points from the same score and Chapter 8’s matched estimate of -4.18 points on the same cohort, it lands between them. That is unsurprising. SMR weighting targets the ATT, as matching did, although it reaches the ATT by retaining the unmatched controls at reduced weight rather than discarding them, so the two ATT estimates need not coincide, and neither sits far from the null. The weights themselves indicate what this costs: among the untreated they average only 0.09 and none exceeds 0.73, because the common arm has to be shrunk substantially to resemble the rare one. The confidence interval widens accordingly, which is the price of asking about the treated rather than about everyone. 9.6 MSMs and where weighting shines The one-covariate regression we fit in the pseudo-population has a name. A marginal structural model is a model for the marginal mean of a potential outcome as a function of treatment, \[E[Y(a)] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 a,\] structural because its arguments are counterfactual treatments rather than observed ones, marginal because it averages over the covariate distribution instead of conditioning on it. The class, and the name, are Robins, Hernán, and Brumback’s (2000). Under the identification conditions, fitting it in the weighted data estimates its parameters, so \(\beta_1\) is the ATE of Chapter 3 — the same estimand standardization targeted, reached by another route. Ours is saturated: with a binary treatment it has one parameter per arm and so cannot be misspecified. Larger MSMs can be, and often carry baseline effect modifiers on the right-hand side to allow subgroup effects. The more important reason to learn weighting is that the framework extends to time-varying treatment, whereas conditioning does not. Suppose patients start and stop a drug over months of follow-up while their covariates evolve. A confounder measured at month six may itself be affected by treatment at month three, making it a mediator as well as a confounder. If we adjust for it in an outcome regression we block part of the effect we are trying to measure and may induce collider bias as well, whereas if we leave it out the later treatment remains confounded. No choice of covariate set resolves that conflict by conditioning, but weighting can: build a weight from a treatment model at each time point, multiply the per-visit weights along each patient’s history, and fit a marginal structural model in the resulting pseudo-population. The time-varying covariates then appear only in the weight models, where they cause no trouble, and never in the outcome model, so nothing is blocked. Chapter 11 applies the same logic to censoring rather than treatment, and Chapter 12 uses it to emulate trials with sustained strategies; much of Part III consists of variations on this chapter. 9.7 Three estimators, one estimand Part II asked one question three times. Here are the answers, with the crude comparison for reference. The standardization row re-runs standardize() with Chapter 7’s seed, so its bootstrap interval reproduces that chapter’s exactly. source("R/standardize.R") crude <- ns |> group_by(cox2_init) |> summarise(r = mean(pud), .groups = "drop") |> pull(r) std <- standardize(ns, reformulate(c("cox2_init", ns_covs), "pud"), treat = "cox2_init", n_boot = 200, seed = 921) ipw <- iptw_estimator(ns, ps_model, outcome = "pud", treat = "cox2_init") pick <- function(d, what, col) d[[col]][d[[1]] == what] comparison <- tibble( estimator = c("Crude", "Standardization (Ch. 7)", "IPTW, stabilized"), estimand = c("none (confounded)", "ATE", "ATE"), rd_pp = 100 * c(crude[2] - crude[1], pick(std, "rd", "estimate"), pick(ipw, "cox2_init", "estimate")), lower = 100 * c(NA, pick(std, "rd", "conf_low"), pick(ipw, "cox2_init", "conf.low")), upper = 100 * c(NA, pick(std, "rd", "conf_high"), pick(ipw, "cox2_init", "conf.high")) ) comparison |> knitr::kable(digits = 2) estimator estimand rd_pp lower upper Crude none (confounded) 2.73 NA NA Standardization (Ch. 7) ATE -0.55 -3.79 2.50 IPTW, stabilized ATE -0.29 -4.21 3.64 The crude risk difference of +2.7 percentage points is the confounded starting point, and both adjusted estimators pull it across the null: standardization to -0.55 points and IPTW to -0.29. The agreement is expected rather than coincidental. Both target the ATE, both use the same nineteen covariates, and both rest on the same identification assumptions; they differ only in which nuisance model carries the load — an outcome model for pud in Chapter 7, a treatment model for cox2_init here. That two estimators relying on different nuisance models land in the same place is mild evidence that neither model is badly wrong, although it is not evidence that the assumptions hold, since both would be wrong together if ns_covs were missing an important confounder. Chapter 8’s matched analysis, recomputed here, gave a risk difference of -4.2 percentage points, further from the null than either of these, which is not a contradiction, since matching targeted the ATT, as the SMR weights above did, averaging over the older and sicker Cox-2 initiators rather than over the whole cohort, and did so using roughly a sixth of the data. Its confidence interval overlaps these comfortably. All three estimators agree on the shape of the answer. The crude signal of harm is confounding, and once the arms are made comparable the estimates hover near the null, with intervals wide enough to admit either a modest benefit or a modest harm. With 288 ulcer cases and 240 Cox-2 initiators, that is as far as these data can take us, and no alternative estimator would sharpen the conclusion, since a better estimator cannot supply information the cohort does not contain. 9.8 Exercises Rerun iptw_estimator() with stabilize = FALSE and compare the point estimate, the standard error, and the weight distribution to the stabilized version. The estimate and its robust standard error will be unchanged; explain why stabilization cannot matter for a saturated marginal structural model, and describe a setting — an MSM with effect modifiers, or the time-varying weights of Chapter 11 — where it would. Drop five covariates from ns_covs to misspecify the treatment model — take arthritis, corticosteroid_use, aspirin_use, ppi_use, and h2_antagonist_use, all plausible confounders — and rerun the estimator. Report the maximum stabilized weight and the risk difference under both covariate sets. Which moves more, the estimate or the weight distribution, and what does that tell you about using weight diagnostics to detect an inadequate adjustment set? Formalize what the SMR section did by hand: write iptw_att(), a copy of iptw_estimator() in which treated patients receive weight 1 and untreated patients receive ps / (1 - ps). Confirm that it reproduces the SMR-weighted estimate above, then compare it with Chapter 8’s matched estimate. Why is stabilization unnecessary for these weights, and which arm’s weights now carry the long tail? In ns the ATE and ATT estimates above sit close together, which is a fact about this cohort rather than a general result. Kurth and colleagues (2006, AJE) analyzed thrombolysis with t-PA and mortality after ischemic stroke, where the treatment effect varied sharply with baseline stroke severity, and found that IPTW and SMR weighting of the same cohort gave sharply different answers, far apart enough that a reader would draw different conclusions from the two. Using this chapter’s vocabulary, explain which patients dominate the weighted comparison under each scheme, and why effect heterogeneity turns the choice between them from a technical preference into a substantive one. Then say which of the two you would specify in advance for a question about whether to start treatment in a patient who currently would not receive it, and which for a question about whether current prescribing practice is doing harm.
